formulas.title: §1245 recapture — $5,000 tractor sale
formulas.formula: Adjusted basis = original basis − depreciation; gain = sale proceeds − adjusted basis
formulas.meaning: An asset with $4k remaining basis sold for $5k creates $1k taxable gain that recaptures earlier depreciation.
formulas.laymanExplanation: An asset with $4k remaining basis sold for $5k creates $1k taxable gain that recaptures earlier depreciation.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Cost=$10,000. Step 2: Deductions allowed/allowable=$6,000, adjusted basis=$4,000. Step 3: Sell=$5,000 ⇒ gain=$1,000. Step 4: Ordinary recapture=min(gain $1,000, depreciation $6,000)=$1,000 under §1245.
formulas.source: Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 9 assigned pp.397; constructed calculations explicitly distinguished.

formulas.title: §1245 recapture — $11,000 tractor sale
formulas.formula: Ordinary recapture = min(realized gain, prior depreciation); excess gain separately characterized
formulas.meaning: When sale proceeds exceed original cost, the extra profit after recapture may receive different character.
formulas.laymanExplanation: When sale proceeds exceed original cost, the extra profit after recapture may receive different character.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Cost $10k−depreciation $6k=adjusted basis $4k. Step 2: Sell $11k → total gain $7k. Step 3: §1245 ordinary recapture=min($7k,$6k)=$6k. Step 4: Remaining $1k may be §1231 gain subject to further applicable netting/character rules, not automatically preferential capital gain.
formulas.source: Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 9 assigned pp.397; constructed calculations explicitly distinguished.

formulas.title: Straight-line depreciation percentage
formulas.formula: Annual percentage ≈ 100% ÷ useful life
formulas.meaning: A five-year straight-line recovery uses about one-fifth each year, before tax conventions.
formulas.laymanExplanation: A five-year straight-line recovery uses about one-fifth each year, before tax conventions.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Original asset basis $10,000, hypothetical 5-year period and zero salvage. Step 2: Annual percentage 1/5=20%; deduction $10,000×20%=$2,000 in each full year before conventions. Step 3: MACRS accelerated methods and first-year conventions may change actual statutory schedule.
formulas.source: Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 9 assigned pp.396–399; constructed calculations explicitly distinguished.

formulas.title: 200% declining balance — general mechanism
formulas.formula: Tentative depreciation = 2 × (1/recovery years) × remaining adjusted basis
formulas.meaning: An accelerated method takes larger deductions near the beginning.
formulas.laymanExplanation: An accelerated method takes larger deductions near the beginning.
formulas.worked: Constructed simplified illustration without tax conventions: 5-year property, beginning basis $10,000. First-year 200% DB tentative rate=2/5=40%, tentative deduction $4,000 (actual MACRS half-year convention would ordinarily alter first year); remaining $6,000. Subsequent years apply rate to remaining basis, switching to straight line when optimal. This is METHOD ILLUSTRATION not assigned rate table.
formulas.source: Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 9 assigned pp.399–400; constructed calculations explicitly distinguished.

formulas.title: §197 15-year intangible amortization
formulas.formula: Annual §197 amount ≈ capitalized eligible basis / 15; monthly = basis/180
formulas.meaning: Spread qualifying purchased goodwill cost evenly over 180 months.
formulas.laymanExplanation: Spread qualifying purchased goodwill cost evenly over 180 months.
formulas.worked: Constructed example: acquired eligible §197 intangible costs $180,000. Monthly amortization=$180,000/180=$1,000. Twelve full months would be $12,000; first year depends on acquisition month, eligibility and exclusions.
formulas.source: Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 9 assigned pp.401–405; constructed calculations explicitly distinguished.

formulas.title: Wash sale loss and replacement basis
formulas.formula: Deferred wash loss = old basis − loss sale proceeds; replacement basis ≈ new purchase price + deferred loss
formulas.meaning: When you sell a losing stock and quickly repurchase it, the loss generally follows the new shares.
formulas.laymanExplanation: When you sell a losing stock and quickly repurchase it, the loss generally follows the new shares.
formulas.worked: Textbook: initial share basis=$100, sale=$60, disallowed loss=$40. Replacement bought at $60⇒new basis $100; bought at $61⇒basis $101; bought at $59⇒basis $99. The actual loss remains deferred until qualifying later disposition.
formulas.source: Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 9 assigned pp.408–409; constructed calculations explicitly distinguished.

formulas.title: Loss measurement limited by adjusted basis
formulas.formula: Potential §165 deductible loss ≤ adjusted basis, subject to compensations and applicable tests
formulas.meaning: Your loss deduction doesn't include property value you never paid tax on.
formulas.laymanExplanation: Your loss deduction doesn't include property value you never paid tax on.
formulas.worked: Book: business building adjusted basis $100,000, FMV $1 million. Destroyed by hurricane with no insurance; basis limits potential §165 loss to $100,000, before other statutory limits.
formulas.source: Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 9 assigned pp.409–410; constructed calculations explicitly distinguished.

formulas.title: §199A 20% QBI and effective marginal rate
formulas.formula: QBI deduction = qualifying income ×20% (before limitations); adjusted rate ≈ 80% × marginal tax rate
formulas.meaning: A $1m qualifying business profit can receive $200k deduction, reducing taxable amount to $800k.
formulas.laymanExplanation: A $1m qualifying business profit can receive $200k deduction, reducing taxable amount to $800k.
formulas.worked: Book simplified illustration: qualifying QBI=$1,000,000, allowable 20% deduction=$200,000; remaining ordinary taxable base $800,000. At flat illustrative 37% marginal rate tax=$296,000 instead of $370,000, effective burden=29.6%. Actual §199A thresholds/limits apply.
formulas.source: Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 9 assigned pp.410–412; constructed calculations explicitly distinguished.

formulas.title: §199A wages or wages-plus-property limit
formulas.formula: Limit = greater of 50% W-2 wages OR 25% W-2 wages + 2.5% UBIA
formulas.meaning: The amount a business pays workers or invests in qualifying property can limit its QBI deduction.
formulas.laymanExplanation: The amount a business pays workers or invests in qualifying property can limit its QBI deduction.
formulas.worked: Constructed example before other limits: W-2 wages=$100,000, qualifying property UBIA=$1,000,000. Option 1=50%×$100,000=$50,000. Option 2=25%×$100,000 +2.5%×$1,000,000=$25,000+$25,000=$50,000. Wage/property cap=$50,000, before QBI/taxable-income ceilings. Applicable threshold test required.
formulas.source: Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 9 assigned pp.411; constructed calculations explicitly distinguished.

formulas.title: Three dimes for a quarter — apparent after-tax profit
formulas.formula: Claimed net tax benefit = deduction × marginal rate − net economic loss
formulas.meaning: A tax-loss gimmick may appear profitable even when its actual transaction loses money.
formulas.laymanExplanation: A tax-loss gimmick may appear profitable even when its actual transaction loses money.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Pay $300,000, receive $250,000 => pretax net loss $50,000. Step 2: If full $300,000 were deductible at 40%, hypothetical tax saving=$120,000. Step 3: If $250,000 receipt were completely excluded, hypothetical after-tax net=$120,000−$50,000=$70,000. Step 4: Casebook calls scheme probably not allowable; this is math to spot arbitrage, NOT approval of deduction.
formulas.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 9 Chapter 8 pp.413–414. Calculated examples explicitly distinguish textbook numbers from constructed figures.

formulas.title: Knetsch 3.5% loan versus 2.5% annuity spread
formulas.formula: Interest paid=principal×3.5%; annual annuity growth≈principal×2.5%; pretax spread=−1%×principal
formulas.meaning: The loan's borrowing cost exceeded the return from the annuity even before tax.
formulas.laymanExplanation: The loan's borrowing cost exceeded the return from the annuity even before tax.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Annuity/debt face base $4,000,000. Step 2: Annual 3.5% interest=$140,000. Step 3: 2.5% annual credit=$100,000. Step 4: $100,000−$140,000=−$40,000 before any insurance company/transaction fees. Step 5: Tax savings only if claimed interest deduction valid, which Court denied.
formulas.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 9 Chapter 8 pp.421–424. Calculated examples explicitly distinguish textbook numbers from constructed figures.

formulas.title: Knetsch 1953 actual deduction and 1954 claim
formulas.meaning: The insurer issued a small additional loan and charged a second advance-interest amount.
formulas.laymanExplanation: The insurer issued a small additional loan and charged a second advance-interest amount.
formulas.worked: Step 1: 1953 principal interest on $4m=$140,000. Step 2: Second $99,000 borrow-back note interest at 3.5%=$3,465. Step 3: 1953 total claimed=$143,465. Step 4: 1954 existing aggregate debt interest=$143,465, plus $104k new loan interest=$3,640; total claimed=$147,105. Step 5: Both claims denied under sham-debt theory.
formulas.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 9 Chapter 8 pp.421–423. Calculated examples explicitly distinguish textbook numbers from constructed figures.

formulas.title: Knetsch after-tax outcomes by hypothetical rate
formulas.formula: Pretax cost $140,000−$100,000=$40,000; after-tax outcome = tax rate × $140,000 − $40,000
formulas.meaning: The higher someone's bracket, the more profitable a deductible fake loss would look.
formulas.laymanExplanation: The higher someone's bracket, the more profitable a deductible fake loss would look.
formulas.worked: Step 1: 90% bracket -> $126,000 claimed saving -> $86,000 net. Step 2: 70% -> $98,000 saving -> $58,000 net. Step 3: 50% -> $70,000 saving -> $30,000 net. Step 4: 25% -> $35,000 saving -> −$5,000 net. Textbook table ignores $4k fee and later tax; deductions were rejected.
formulas.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 9 Chapter 8 pp.424–425. Calculated examples explicitly distinguish textbook numbers from constructed figures.

formulas.title: Knetsch source arithmetic discrepancy warning
formulas.formula: Printed 'paid $294,540 − loans $203,000 = difference $91,570' does not reconcile
formulas.meaning: The casebook extract contains a $30 mismatch; don't memorize an inconsistent calculation.
formulas.laymanExplanation: The casebook extract contains a $30 mismatch; don't memorize an inconsistent calculation.
formulas.worked: The assigned quoted opinion states $294,540 payments and $203,000 borrowed back but says $91,570 out of pocket. Direct subtraction is $91,540, while $143,465+$147,105+$4,000=$294,570, which DOES yield $91,570 after subtracting $203,000. This is a source arithmetic/transcription inconsistency; use the separately shown interest/payment components and label discrepancy rather than silently 'correcting' the case.
formulas.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 9 Chapter 8 pp.423. Calculated examples explicitly distinguish textbook numbers from constructed figures.

formulas.title: Historic rental shelter: break-even cash, $12,000 paper loss
formulas.formula: Taxable result=rent after costs before interest − interest − depreciation
formulas.meaning: The building broke even economically, but depreciation created a paper tax loss.
formulas.laymanExplanation: The building broke even economically, but depreciation created a paper tax loss.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Borrow $100,000 at 9%; interest=$9,000. Step 2: Rental return before interest after other costs=$9,000. Step 3: $9,000−$9,000=$0 cash/economic result (assuming no change in value). Step 4: Add allowed depreciation of $12,000 under historic assumption → taxable loss=−$12,000. Step 5: Basis falls $100,000→$88,000; sale at $100,000 gives $12,000 realization gain, potentially deferring earlier deduction.
formulas.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 9 Chapter 8 pp.428–429. Calculated examples explicitly distinguish textbook numbers from constructed figures.

formulas.title: §163(d) investment-interest carryforward
formulas.formula: Current investment interest deductible ≤ net investment income; excess carried forward
formulas.meaning: Stock going up in price isn't the same as investment interest income that unlocks a deduction.
formulas.laymanExplanation: Stock going up in price isn't the same as investment interest income that unlocks a deduction.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Book illustration borrow $100,000 at 10% => $10,000 annual interest. Step 2: Stock appreciates 15% but pays $0 dividend; generally current investment income is $0, so $10,000 interest deduction is carried forward. Step 3: In year 2, another $10,000 interest paid and $20,000 eligible dividends received; if all other conditions met, $20,000 current/prior investment interest can be deducted. This is SOURCE NARRATIVE example, NOT Stan's p433 assigned problem.
formulas.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 9 Chapter 8 pp.431–432. Calculated examples explicitly distinguish textbook numbers from constructed figures.

formulas.title: §465 at-risk loss ceiling
formulas.formula: Currently deductible qualifying loss ≤ amount at risk (before other restrictions)
formulas.meaning: Borrowing large nonrecourse sums doesn't automatically mean the whole borrowed amount is truly at risk.
formulas.laymanExplanation: Borrowing large nonrecourse sums doesn't automatically mean the whole borrowed amount is truly at risk.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Book illustration acquire motion picture for $2 million. Step 2: Pay $200,000 own cash and issue $1,800,000 nonrecourse note secured only by film. Step 3: Subject to §465 (with no exception), at-risk amount may be only $200,000. Step 4: Loss deductions above available at-risk amount suspended; §469 may independently restrict losses.
formulas.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 9 Chapter 8 pp.432–433. Calculated examples explicitly distinguish textbook numbers from constructed figures.

formulas.title: §265 borrowing to hold tax-exempt bonds — constructed illustration
formulas.formula: Interest expense = loan × borrowing rate; net return = tax-exempt yield − nondeductible interest
formulas.meaning: Tax law stops deducting interest used to earn income that is itself excluded.
formulas.laymanExplanation: Tax law stops deducting interest used to earn income that is itself excluded.
formulas.worked: Constructed dollar example based on assigned rate comparison: borrow $100,000 at 8% to buy tax-exempt bonds yielding 7%; annual cost=$8,000 and tax-free bond interest=$7,000, economic loss=$1,000. Section 265(a)(2) generally denies the $8,000 borrowing-interest deduction; cannot claim after-tax gain by deducting cost against other income.
formulas.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 9 Chapter 8 pp.427–428, 432. Calculated examples explicitly distinguish textbook numbers from constructed figures.

formulas.title: Individual AMT simplified comparison — historical schedule
formulas.formula: Additional AMT due=max(0, tentative AMT − regular tax)
formulas.meaning: You don't pay both full taxes. You pay whichever computation requires more total tax.
formulas.laymanExplanation: You don't pay both full taxes. You pay whichever computation requires more total tax.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Use book's 2022 single-filer AMT exemption $75,900, and 26% tax tier; historical method, not 2026 amount. Step 2: CONSTRUCTED example regular taxable income $150,000, AMT preferences $50,000, no phaseout: AMTI=$150,000+$50,000−$75,900=$124,100. Step 3: Simplified tentative AMT=$124,100×26%=$32,266 (ignoring other AMT foreign tax credit/adjustments). Step 4: If assumed regular tax=$30,000, additional AMT=$2,266. Actual 2026 thresholds differ.
formulas.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 9 Chapter 8 pp.433–434. Calculated examples explicitly distinguish textbook numbers from constructed figures.

formulas.title: §7701(o) penalties — constructed underpayment
formulas.formula: Economic-substance penalty = underpayment ×20% (or 40% if nondisclosed)
formulas.meaning: Disallowing a shelter can lead to an extra penalty on top of the tax bill.
formulas.laymanExplanation: Disallowing a shelter can lead to an extra penalty on top of the tax bill.
formulas.worked: CONSTRUCTED illustration: disallowed tax-benefit underpayment $50,000. Penalty if relevant disclosed transaction=20%×$50,000=$10,000. If not adequately disclosed=40%×$50,000=$20,000. Separate interest/other liabilities not included. §6664(c)(2) eliminates ordinary reasonable-cause defense for this penalty.
formulas.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 9 Chapter 8 pp.438–439. Calculated examples explicitly distinguish textbook numbers from constructed figures.

formulas.title: Pevsner — costs claimed versus allowed
formulas.formula: Wardrobe $1,381.91 + upkeep $240 = $1,621.91 attempted deduction
formulas.meaning: Pevsner spent over $1,600 on apparel for boutique job but received no allowable deduction.
formulas.laymanExplanation: Pevsner spent over $1,600 on apparel for boutique job but received no allowable deduction.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Apparel cost $1,381.91. Step 2: Upkeep $240. Step 3: Combined claim $1,621.91. Step 4: Fifth Circuit denied both because garments were objectively adaptable to ordinary use; amount claimed not equivalent to deductible amount.
formulas.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 9 Chapter 9 pp.448–450; constructed illustrations explicitly identified.

formulas.title: Popov — original claimed proportions, not confirmed award
formulas.formula: Claimed rent = total annual rent ×40%; electricity = annual electricity×20%
formulas.meaning: The violinist allocated 40% of rent and 20% electricity, but the case primarily decided entitlement.
formulas.laymanExplanation: The violinist allocated 40% of rent and 20% electricity, but the case primarily decided entitlement.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Source provides percentages, not underlying total rent/electric bills. Step 2: Example algebra: annual rent R; claimed 0.40R. Annual electricity E; claimed 0.20E. Step 3: Court held she qualified for a home-office deduction; source does not establish final approved dollar allocations. Do not invent R/E values.
formulas.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 9 Chapter 9 pp.452–455; constructed illustrations explicitly identified.

formulas.title: Home-office allocation — constructed illustration
formulas.formula: Business area ratio = exclusive qualifying office square feet / total home square feet
formulas.meaning: A small dedicated qualifying business room may support allocating a share of home expenses.
formulas.laymanExplanation: A small dedicated qualifying business room may support allocating a share of home expenses.
formulas.worked: CONSTRUCTED example, not Popov's facts: home 1,200 sq ft, office 180 sq ft, ratio 180/1,200=15%. Annual otherwise allocable home costs $24,000 ⇒ initial 15% ×$24,000=$3,600 before statutory income ceilings, depreciation and other §280A allocation rules. Must qualify under exclusive/regular tests.
formulas.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 9 Chapter 9 pp.451–456; constructed illustrations explicitly identified.

formulas.title: Modern simplified office deduction — external IRS annotation
formulas.formula: Deduction ≈ min(qualifying area, 300 sq ft) × $5, subject to income cap
formulas.meaning: If you qualify for the simplified home office option, multiply area by five dollars.
formulas.laymanExplanation: If you qualify for the simplified home office option, multiply area by five dollars.
formulas.worked: CONSTRUCTED post-textbook illustration (IRS IRS Pub.587, NOT in casebook): dedicated qualifying 200 sq ft ×$5=$1,000, subject to income limits. Max 300×$5=$1,500. Choosing simplified method generally means you cannot separately claim actual office operating expenses/depreciation for same home office. This is external current-law note, not professor-assigned example.
formulas.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 9 Chapter 9 pp.451–456; constructed illustrations explicitly identified.

formulas.title: §280A vacation-home personal-use threshold
formulas.formula: Threshold = max(14 days, 10% × days rented at fair rental)
formulas.meaning: Check 14 days versus ten percent of rented days, and use whichever number is larger.
formulas.laymanExplanation: Check 14 days versus ten percent of rented days, and use whichever number is larger.
formulas.worked: CONSTRUCTED illustration: fair rental 120 days; 10%=12 days, greater of 14 and 12 is 14. If 15 personal days, exceeds threshold and treated as residence; if 14 personal days, not over the threshold. Count relevant family use separately.
formulas.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 9 Chapter 9 pp.456–457; constructed illustrations explicitly identified.

formulas.title: Vacation home rented 250 days — threshold
formulas.formula: max(14 days, 0.10 ×250 rental days)=25 days
formulas.meaning: When a property is rented many days, the ten-percent side can exceed 14 days.
formulas.laymanExplanation: When a property is rented many days, the ten-percent side can exceed 14 days.
formulas.worked: CONSTRUCTED example: fair rental 250 days -> 25 threshold personal days. If personal use 20, does not exceed 25; if 26, exceeds threshold and vacation-residence limits may apply. Do not confuse rented days and personal days.
formulas.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 9 Chapter 9 pp.456–457; constructed illustrations explicitly identified.

formulas.title: §280A(g) fewer than 15 rental days
formulas.formula: Taxable rental receipts=0; rental-only deductions=0 if qualifying residence rented fewer than 15 days
formulas.meaning: A personal-use residence rented just 12 days may exclude those rental receipts entirely.
formulas.laymanExplanation: A personal-use residence rented just 12 days may exclude those rental receipts entirely.
formulas.worked: CONSTRUCTED example: qualifying personal-use residence rented at fair rent 12 days for $12,000 -> excludes $12,000 rental receipts under §280A(g) and cannot deduct expenses attributable to those 12 rental days. Other independent homeowner deductions are analyzed separately. If property rented 15 days, this exclusion does not apply.
formulas.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 9 Chapter 9 pp.456–457; constructed illustrations explicitly identified.

formulas.title: Vacation-home expense allocation — constructed
formulas.formula: Rental-use expense share (simplified) = shared expense × rental days/(rental days+personal use days)
formulas.meaning: Split common costs between time home was rented and time owner used it.
formulas.laymanExplanation: Split common costs between time home was rented and time owner used it.
formulas.worked: CONSTRUCTED training illustration: fair rented 90 days, personal used 30 days; shared annual deductible-eligible operating costs $12,000; preliminary allocation 90/(90+30)=75% -> $9,000 potential rental cost. §280A(c)(5), tax/interest rules and actual method may limit deductible amount. Do not assume §280A 75% always applies to all costs.
formulas.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 9 Chapter 9 pp.456–457; constructed illustrations explicitly identified.

formulas.title: §21 historical book example of credit 35%
formulas.formula: Book max nominal credit for 2+ = $6,000 ×35% = $2,100
formulas.meaning: A 35% credit applied to $6,000 eligible expenses produces $2,100, but only in that historical bracket.
formulas.laymanExplanation: A 35% credit applied to $6,000 eligible expenses produces $2,100, but only in that historical bracket.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Source uses expense ceiling $6,000 for 2+ and high historical 35% credit rate. Step 2: $6,000×0.35=$2,100. Step 3: §21 nonrefundable benefit actually received cannot exceed available tax. Step 4: For 2026, use changed 50% max rate and revised phase-down instead.
formulas.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 10 Chapter 9 pp.461–462; constructed illustrations explicitly identified.

formulas.title: §21 2026 maximum credit (current-law annotation)
formulas.formula: 2026 credit potential = qualifying capped expenses × applicable 20–50% rate
formulas.meaning: At the 2026 highest rate, one child gives up to $1,500 and two or more up to $3,000.
formulas.laymanExplanation: At the 2026 highest rate, one child gives up to $1,500 and two or more up to $3,000.
formulas.worked: External 2026 IRS rate update (not textbook numeric): one qualifying child ceiling $3,000 ×50% = $1,500; two or more ceiling $6,000×50%=$3,000, subject to income phasedown, earned income, provider requirements and nonrefundable tax liability cap. Prior 2021 one-year rules are different.
formulas.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 10 Chapter 9 pp.461–462; constructed illustrations explicitly identified.

formulas.title: §129 employer child-care exclusion tax savings
formulas.formula: Tax saved (approx.) = allowed excluded care benefits × employee marginal income-tax rate
formulas.meaning: Excluding employer daycare benefits saves more in dollars when your marginal rate is higher.
formulas.laymanExplanation: Excluding employer daycare benefits saves more in dollars when your marginal rate is higher.
formulas.worked: CONSTRUCTED 2026 illustration (not source book): qualified DCAP payment $6,000 (below 2026 $7,500 cap), hypothetical marginal federal income tax 24%. Approx income tax saved = $6,000×0.24=$1,440; payroll tax treatment, limitations, other credits and actual brackets may change. No §21 double counting.
formulas.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 10 Chapter 9 pp.461–462; constructed illustrations explicitly identified.

formulas.title: Carroll versus Kopaigora amounts claimed
formulas.formula: Carroll claimed $720.80; Kopaigora claimed $18,879
formulas.meaning: A small or large tuition bill doesn't decide deductibility; the purpose/qualification test does.
formulas.laymanExplanation: A small or large tuition bill doesn't decide deductibility; the purpose/qualification test does.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Carroll claimed $720.80 college tuition and deduction was denied under §162. Step 2: Kopaigora claimed $18,879 EMBA expenses and his historic §162 deduction was allowed. Step 3: Different result was based on specific current business skills and new trade qualification—not price. Step 4: In 2026 separately apply employee §67(g) restrictions.
formulas.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 10 Chapter 9 pp.463–467; constructed illustrations explicitly identified.

formulas.title: §127 combined tax-free employer education ceiling
formulas.formula: 2026 qualifying assistance exclusion ≤ $5,250 annually (combined qualifying education and student-loan payments)
formulas.meaning: Your employer's tax-free education and loan-repayment aid share one annual bucket.
formulas.laymanExplanation: Your employer's tax-free education and loan-repayment aid share one annual bucket.
formulas.worked: CONSTRUCTED current-year illustration: employer pays $3,000 eligible student-loan principal and $2,500 eligible tuition in 2026, total $5,500. Combined exclusion at most $5,250, so $250 potentially includible wages absent another rule. Plan/program conditions apply; cap indexed after 2026.
formulas.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 10 Chapter 9 pp.465–469; constructed illustrations explicitly identified.

formulas.title: Hantzis summer work — economic take-home before tax
formulas.formula: Gross $3,750 − away expenses $3,204 = $546
formulas.meaning: The taxpayer earned only $546 more than the cost of traveling and staying in NYC.
formulas.laymanExplanation: The taxpayer earned only $546 more than the cost of traveling and staying in NYC.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Summer New York income=$3,750. Step 2: Travel, meal and rent claimed=$3,204. Step 3: Pretax net cash from NYC summer job=$546. Step 4: First Circuit denied §162(a)(2) travel costs because no business tax home was maintained in Boston. Economic net does NOT determine tax deduction.
formulas.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 10 Chapter 9 pp.480–482; constructed illustrations explicitly identified.

formulas.title: §274(n) standard half-meal deduction
formulas.formula: Qualifying deductible meal cost × 50%
formulas.meaning: Only half of an otherwise allowable work meal generally reduces taxable income.
formulas.laymanExplanation: Only half of an otherwise allowable work meal generally reduces taxable income.
formulas.worked: CONSTRUCTED illustration: client meal $200 otherwise meets §§162/274 conditions; §274(n) 50% reduction → $100 deduction. If it was an ordinary personal lunch like Moss's, qualifying cost is $0, therefore deduction remains $0—not $100.
formulas.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 10 Chapter 9 pp.492–494; constructed illustrations explicitly identified.

formulas.title: Gilmore cost and source court's 80% allocation
formulas.formula: $40,611.36 × 80% ≈ $32,489 (court below allowed roughly $32,500); Supreme Court denied
formulas.meaning: A lower court allocated most divorce fees to protecting stock, but the Supreme Court rejected the entire business-character theory.
formulas.laymanExplanation: A lower court allocated most divorce fees to protecting stock, but the Supreme Court rejected the entire business-character theory.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Gilmore legal fees total $40,611.36. Step 2: Lower court thought 80% connected to stock protection: 0.80×$40,611.36=$32,489.09 (~$32,500). Step 3: Supreme Court applied marital origin-of-claim test, not allocation by possible investment consequences; denied current §212(2) deduction for fees at issue.
formulas.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 10 Chapter 9 pp.495–499; constructed illustrations explicitly identified.
