entries.title: Blair v. Commissioner
entries.summary: No. The Supreme Court held the children, not Blair, taxable on income from the validly transferred beneficial interests.
entries.laymanExplanation: Blair gave his children actual ownership shares of his lifetime trust-income right, so they—not he—were taxed on income from those interests.
entries.legalExplanation: A genuine present assignment of a substantial interest in income-producing trust property can shift taxation of later income to its transferee.
entries.details: Opinion reproduced in the syllabus-assigned pages.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), syllabus Week 7 reproduced Chapter 6 pp.333–335
entries.sourceRole: Assigned textbook pages, not subsequent unassigned portions
entries.facts: A father created a trust giving his son Blair the income of the trust for life. Blair made formal assignments to his children of specified annual amounts out of his life-income interest, without retaining the assigned rights. Trustees recognized the assignments and paid the children directly. The transfer was valid under governing law.
entries.issue: Was Blair still taxable on trust income allocated to children by valid assignment of part of his equitable beneficial ownership?
entries.holding: No. The Supreme Court held the children, not Blair, taxable on income from the validly transferred beneficial interests.
entries.reasoning: Blair owned a transferable equitable property interest in the trust corpus, including enforcement rights. The children became owners of portions of that interest, not merely agents receiving checks for Blair. This was not assignment of personal-service compensation or an attempt to shift income from property still owned by donor.
entries.rule: A genuine present assignment of a substantial interest in income-producing trust property can shift taxation of later income to its transferee.
entries.exam: Look for irrevocability, full duration, property rights and whether donor retains income source. Contrast Horst's isolated coupon gifts.
entries.examApplication: Look for irrevocability, full duration, property rights and whether donor retains income source. Contrast Horst's isolated coupon gifts.
entries.examTrap: A bare instruction to a trustee to send payments, without actual property-interest transfer, is not enough under Blair.

entries.title: Helvering v. Horst
entries.summary: No. The Supreme Court reversed and held the father taxable on the interest paid to the son.
entries.laymanExplanation: The dad kept the bond but gave his son this year's interest coupons. The Court said the interest was still the dad's taxable income.
entries.legalExplanation: An owner who retains the income-producing asset and merely directs/assigns its income to another may remain taxable on the income when it is paid.
entries.details: Opinion reproduced in the syllabus-assigned pages.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), syllabus Week 7 reproduced Chapter 6 pp.335–338
entries.sourceRole: Assigned textbook pages, not subsequent unassigned portions
entries.facts: The owner of negotiable bonds detached upcoming interest coupons shortly before they matured and gave them to his son, while retaining ownership of the bonds. The son collected the coupons when paid that year. The donor was on the cash-receipts method and did not physically receive the interest.
entries.issue: May a bond owner avoid tax on interest by giving his son coupons before payment while retaining ownership of the principal bond?
entries.holding: No. The Supreme Court reversed and held the father taxable on the interest paid to the son.
entries.reasoning: The father controlled the income-producing investment and exercised his right to enjoy its return by directing interest to his son, satisfying a personal objective. Economic enjoyment of accrued income need not be physical receipt. Blair was different because that case transferred the income-producing beneficial property itself.
entries.rule: An owner who retains the income-producing asset and merely directs/assigns its income to another may remain taxable on the income when it is paid.
entries.exam: Identify retained property source, gift of income only, cash versus accrual timing; distinguish bona fide underlying property transfer in Blair.
entries.examApplication: Identify retained property source, gift of income only, cash versus accrual timing; distinguish bona fide underlying property transfer in Blair.
entries.examTrap: No physical receipt is required; distinguish legitimate gift of underlying bond from assignment of its short-term interest coupons.

topics.title: A. Assignment of Income — Income-Producing Property
topics.description: Source property versus assigned receipts, Blair and Horst, §1286 interest stripping, and the Kiddie Tax.

entries.title: Gross receipts vs. net business income
entries.summary: Gross receipts are total sales; business profit accounts for cost of goods and deductible expenses.
entries.laymanExplanation: A store collecting $1 million isn't making $1 million in profit if it spent $900,000 to make those sales.
entries.legalExplanation: The text illustrates $1m revenue less $600k merchandise costs, $140k employees and $160k rent/utilities = $100k net business income. Distinguish costs of inventory from immediately deductible costs because timing rules affect recognition.
entries.details: The text illustrates $1m revenue less $600k merchandise costs, $140k employees and $160k rent/utilities = $100k net business income. Distinguish costs of inventory from immediately deductible costs because timing rules affect recognition.

entries.title: Only net income is the proper income-tax base
entries.summary: Business costs of earning revenue generally reduce the amount of taxable economic income, while personal consumption generally does not.
entries.laymanExplanation: Buying groceries to resell is a cost of making money. Buying food to eat yourself is normally spending your income.
entries.legalExplanation: The net income principle motivates deduction of ordinary business outlays, subject to the capitalization, timing and statutory limitation provisions. Business versus personal costs invokes §§162 and 262.
entries.details: The net income principle motivates deduction of ordinary business outlays, subject to the capitalization, timing and statutory limitation provisions. Business versus personal costs invokes §§162 and 262.

entries.title: Adjusted gross income (AGI)
entries.summary: Gross income minus qualifying deductions listed in §62(a).
entries.laymanExplanation: AGI is an intermediate subtotal before most personal deductions.
entries.legalExplanation: Section 62 defines AGI by specific above-the-line deductions. Examples include self-employed trade/business costs, rent/royalty income costs and specified employee categories. AGI generally precedes standard/itemized deductions.
entries.details: Section 62 defines AGI by specific above-the-line deductions. Examples include self-employed trade/business costs, rent/royalty income costs and specified employee categories. AGI generally precedes standard/itemized deductions.

entries.title: Above-the-line deductions — §62
entries.summary: Deductions subtracted to determine AGI; often self-employment, business and other specially listed costs.
entries.laymanExplanation: You subtract these before reaching AGI, generally whether or not you itemize.
entries.legalExplanation: Above-the-line is an informal term; typical §62(a)(1) expenses are tied to a trade/business carried on other than as an employee. Special above-line categories for employees and capital losses are separate.
entries.details: Above-the-line is an informal term; typical §62(a)(1) expenses are tied to a trade/business carried on other than as an employee. Special above-line categories for employees and capital losses are separate.

entries.title: Below-the-line deductions — §63
entries.summary: Deductions subtracted after AGI, commonly standard or itemized deductions plus statutorily specified other deductions.
entries.laymanExplanation: Below the line is the next stage of reducing taxable income, after AGI.
entries.legalExplanation: An individual generally chooses standard deduction under §63(c) or itemized deductions under §63(d), rather than both, with additional qualifying deductions as statute provides. Source also mentions §151 exemptions suspended through 2025, §199A, and §170(p).

entries.title: Tax schedules — Schedule C, A, D, E and F
entries.summary: Different schedules report business profit, itemized deductions, capital transactions, supplemental income and farm profit.
entries.laymanExplanation: The Schedule is the worksheet where items go; it doesn't by itself decide whether they're deductible.
entries.legalExplanation: Schedule C covers sole proprietors; A personal itemized; D capital gain/loss; E rents, royalties and pass-through income; F farming. Underlying Code rules control deductibility and tax treatment.

entries.title: Self-employed versus employee expense deductions
entries.summary: Self-employed business expenses are often above-the-line, while most unreimbursed employee business expenses are more restricted.
entries.laymanExplanation: Two people incur identical work costs, but the freelancer may deduct them while a regular employee may not.
entries.legalExplanation: The casebook describes pre-2026 suspension of many unreimbursed employee business itemized deductions. Certain §62(a)(2) specified employees remain eligible for above-the-line treatment; ordinary salaried employees generally do not.

entries.title: §162 — current deduction of ordinary and necessary business expenses
entries.summary: Ordinary and necessary costs paid or incurred while carrying on a trade or business may be deducted unless another rule requires capitalization or disallows them.
entries.laymanExplanation: Routine operating costs like paying workers, supplies or business rent often reduce income now.
entries.legalExplanation: Section 162(a) requires ordinary, necessary expenses paid/incurred in taxable year while carrying on an existing trade or business; §263 may require capitalization, §262 blocks personal spending and other provisions limit categories.
entries.details: Section 162(a) requires ordinary, necessary expenses paid/incurred in taxable year while carrying on an existing trade or business; §263 may require capitalization, §262 blocks personal spending and other provisions limit categories.

entries.elements: Expense; ordinary; necessary; paid/incurred in taxable year; carrying on trade or business; not capital or otherwise disallowed.
entries.examTrap: Just because a cost benefits a business does not automatically make it immediately deductible.

entries.title: §262 — personal, family, living expenses nondeductible
entries.summary: Personal consumption expenses are generally excluded from business deductions.
entries.laymanExplanation: You generally can't deduct personal shopping as a cost of running your business.
entries.legalExplanation: Section 262 prevents deductions for personal, family and living outlays even where taxpayer has some incidental benefit; analyze mixed-purpose costs under applicable tracing and limitations.
entries.details: Section 262 prevents deductions for personal, family and living outlays even where taxpayer has some incidental benefit; analyze mixed-purpose costs under applicable tracing and limitations.

entries.title: §263 — capitalize acquisition/improvement of long-lived property
entries.summary: A building, machinery or permanent improvement often must be added to basis instead of immediately deducted.
entries.laymanExplanation: Buying a factory is buying an asset, not merely paying this year's bills.
entries.legalExplanation: Section 263(a) requires capitalization of capital acquisition and specified improvement expenditures; taxpayer may recover capitalized cost through depreciation, amortization or disposition as separately provided. Compare §162 immediate expenses.
entries.details: Section 263(a) requires capitalization of capital acquisition and specified improvement expenditures; taxpayer may recover capitalized cost through depreciation, amortization or disposition as separately provided. Compare §162 immediate expenses.

entries.examApplication: Ask whether money restores current operations or creates/enhances a future capital asset.

entries.title: Matching principle
entries.summary: Align the deduction for an asset's cost with the years when it produces income.
entries.laymanExplanation: A machine lasting five years ideally contributes a share of its cost to expenses in each of those five years.
entries.legalExplanation: The book contrasts paying $10k upfront for a five-year machine versus renting for $2k each year; capitalization plus cost recovery approximates economic matching. The statute often accelerates depreciation for incentives.
entries.details: The book contrasts paying $10k upfront for a five-year machine versus renting for $2k each year; capitalization plus cost recovery approximates economic matching. The statute often accelerates depreciation for incentives.

entries.title: §263A UNICAP — production costs included in inventory/basis
entries.summary: Direct and allocable indirect production costs generally must be capitalized into inventory or self-created qualifying property.
entries.laymanExplanation: The salary of factory workers and part of factory overhead may become part of the goods' cost until those goods sell.
entries.legalExplanation: §263A applies to qualifying producers and certain resale businesses, requiring both direct and indirect production costs to be assigned to property. Sales/marketing and some general planning expenses may be excepted; small-business exceptions depend on current gross receipts test.

entries.legalExplanation: Reg. §1.263(a)-3 includes material capacity/productivity increases, restoration of disrepair, and adaptation to new/different use. Compare property's condition before the event necessitating expense.

entries.summary: Otherwise deductible remediation may have to be capitalized into manufactured inventory as indirect production costs.

entries.legalExplanation: Rev. Rul. 94-38 permits §162 cleanup rather than land improvement on the specified facts; Rev. Rul. 2004-18 says §263A can nevertheless require allocating remediation to inventory and deducting cost when inventory sells.

entries.title: Midland Empire Packing Co. v. Commissioner
entries.summary: The Tax Court permitted an immediate $4,868.81 business expense deduction as a repair.
entries.laymanExplanation: A meat-packing business lined its basement with concrete because a neighboring refinery's oil seepage threatened the plant. Court allowed deduction for repair.
entries.details: Reproduced opinion within the assigned casebook pages.
entries.facts: Midland used its basement for 25 years to cure meats and store hides. A new refinery released oil that seeped into the basement, creating odors/fire hazard and threatening government meat inspectors' approval. Midland spent $4,868.81 on a concrete wall and floor lining that did not expand the space, increase productive capacity or extend original useful life.
entries.issue: Was concrete oil-proofing a currently deductible ordinary and necessary repair under §162, or a capital improvement under §263?
entries.holding: The Tax Court permitted an immediate $4,868.81 business expense deduction as a repair.
entries.reasoning: Work restored ordinary efficient use and prevented a new nuisance, without materially extending original life or creating new use or capacity. Unusual circumstances did not defeat ordinary character. Court did not need to reach alternative loss claim.
entries.rule: A cost primarily restoring property to the same normal operating condition without adding significant new value, life or use can qualify as a repair expense.
entries.exam: Compare pre-damage and post-repair building function; first identify unit of property, then betterment/restoration/adaptation tests under modern regulations.
entries.examApplication: Compare pre-damage and post-repair building function; first identify unit of property, then betterment/restoration/adaptation tests under modern regulations.
entries.examTrap: Not every physical addition is a capital improvement; modern regulation applies more precise BRA framework.
entries.source: Reproduced judicial opinion: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Tax Week 8, pp.370–372

entries.legalExplanation: Welch assumed paying predecessor debts might improve standing (necessary), but denied current deduction as extraordinary reputation/goodwill creation.

entries.title: Expenses from unrelated conduct during business travel
entries.summary: Business trip does not automatically make all incident-related legal costs business deductions.
entries.laymanExplanation: Just because something bad happened on a work trip doesn't make legal costs ordinary business expenses.
entries.legalExplanation: Gilliam found artist's in-flight assault and related criminal defense and settlement costs lacked direct business origin and ordinary character; distinguished ordinary vehicle accidents and direct-business claims.

entries.title: Welch v. Helvering
entries.summary: No. The Supreme Court held the expenditures did not qualify for §162's predecessor's ordinary-business-expense deduction.
entries.laymanExplanation: A grain commission agent voluntarily paid debts of his old bankrupt company to restore his reputation. Court denied immediate deduction.
entries.details: Reproduced opinion within the assigned casebook pages.
entries.facts: After a former grain business went bankrupt and discharged its debts, the taxpayer started his own grain commission agency. To restore standing and customer credit, he paid old corporation's creditors over five years despite lacking a legal obligation. IRS treated expenditures as capital development of reputation/goodwill.
entries.issue: Were payments voluntarily made to old creditors deductible as 'ordinary and necessary' trade or business expenses?
entries.holding: No. The Supreme Court held the expenditures did not qualify for §162's predecessor's ordinary-business-expense deduction.
entries.reasoning: Payments could be helpful or appropriate (necessary), but assuming others' obligations to establish reputation was extraordinary in the relevant trade, and more akin to acquisition of enduring goodwill/capital. 'Ordinary' is assessed in business context, not necessarily frequency in one person's lifetime.
entries.rule: Business expenses must be BOTH ordinary and necessary; acquisition of enduring goodwill may require capitalization rather than current deduction.
entries.exam: Identify exact outlay purpose, current operating defense versus developing goodwill, and whether ordinary in that industry; compare payments protecting existing goodwill discussed in notes.
entries.examApplication: Identify exact outlay purpose, current operating defense versus developing goodwill, and whether ordinary in that industry; compare payments protecting existing goodwill discussed in notes.
entries.examTrap: Ordinary doesn't mean repeated frequently by same taxpayer, and necessary alone is insufficient.
entries.source: Reproduced judicial opinion: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Tax Week 8, pp.377–379
entries.sourceRole: Reproduced assigned opinion, not an incidental cited case

entries.title: Gilliam v. Commissioner
entries.summary: No. The Tax Court sustained IRS denial of §162 deductions, finding the conduct and expenses not ordinary incidents of the artist's trade or business.
entries.laymanExplanation: An artist had a medication-related altercation with a passenger while flying to a teaching engagement. Even though he was on business travel, the legal and settlement costs weren't deductible.
entries.details: Reproduced opinion within the assigned casebook pages.
entries.facts: Artist and art teacher Sam Gilliam took prescribed Dalmane shortly after boarding a work trip to Memphis. He experienced extreme disorientation and injured a fellow passenger on flight. He was acquitted on temporary-insanity grounds, settled civil claim for $3,900, and paid legal fees $9,250 in 1975 plus $9,600 in 1976. He claimed business deductions.
entries.issue: Are criminal defense legal fees and civil settlement incurred after assault aboard a business-flight 'ordinary and necessary' expenses incurred carrying on his art business?
entries.holding: No. The Tax Court sustained IRS denial of §162 deductions, finding the conduct and expenses not ordinary incidents of the artist's trade or business.
entries.reasoning: Business-related travel was necessary context, but an in-flight assault was neither part of the taxpayer's artistic services nor a normal incident of professional aviation business travel. The court distinguished ordinary car accident litigation on business driving and legal matters arising directly from trading/business conduct.
entries.rule: An expense's mere occurrence during a business trip does not automatically make it ordinary or sufficiently connected to carrying on that trade or business.
entries.exam: Apply origin/direct-business connection, distinguish accidental driving from unrelated altercation and from litigation based on conduct directly carrying on business.
entries.examApplication: Apply origin/direct-business connection, distinguish accidental driving from unrelated altercation and from litigation based on conduct directly carrying on business.
entries.examTrap: Criminal acquittal does not alone establish deductibility; whether the expense was paid while on a work trip is not dispositive.
entries.source: Reproduced judicial opinion: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Tax Week 8, pp.380–386
entries.sourceRole: Reproduced assigned opinion, not an incidental cited case

entries.title: Commissioner v. Groetzinger
entries.summary: Yes. The Supreme Court held his continuous, regular, primarily profit-seeking full-time gambling qualified as a trade or business for the provisions at issue.
entries.laymanExplanation: A man spent 60–80 hours per week racing greyhounds as his income source. Even though he didn't sell services to customers, court said it was a trade or business.
entries.details: Reproduced opinion within the assigned casebook pages.
entries.facts: After losing his employment, Groetzinger bet on dog races six days/week for 48 weeks in 1978, studied racing forms for 60–80 hours/week, and kept detailed ledgers. He had $70,000 gross winnings and $72,032 wagers, net loss $2,032. Issue concerned whether those activities were 'trade or business' under the relevant tax provisions.
entries.issue: Does full-time gambling on one's own account constitute carrying on a trade or business without offering goods/services to others?
entries.holding: Yes. The Supreme Court held his continuous, regular, primarily profit-seeking full-time gambling qualified as a trade or business for the provisions at issue.
entries.reasoning: The Code did not define trade or business generally. Court rejected Justice Frankfurter's earlier proposed 'holding oneself out to sell goods/services' limitation. A real pursuit carried on continuously and regularly with principal purpose of income or profit qualified; sporadic hobby would not. Personal investment management is treated differently.
entries.rule: Trade or business generally requires regularity and continuity of profit-oriented activity; selling goods/services to third parties is not invariably required.
entries.exam: Examine full-time participation, intention to live on proceeds, recordkeeping, frequency, profit goal, distinguish passive portfolio management/hobby.
entries.examApplication: Examine full-time participation, intention to live on proceeds, recordkeeping, frequency, profit goal, distinguish passive portfolio management/hobby.
entries.examTrap: Trade/business classification does not override separate statutory limitation on gambling loss deductions.
entries.source: Reproduced judicial opinion: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Tax Week 8, pp.387–392

entries.title: Gregory v. Helvering (Second Circuit and Supreme Court)
entries.summary: No. Both courts held the plan lacked the corporate-reorganization character contemplated by Congress and was a device for a stock distribution rather than a genuine reorganization.
entries.laymanExplanation: Mrs. Gregory formed a company, transferred appreciated shares into it, liquidated the shell three days later, then sold the shares. Courts rejected the claimed tax-free corporate reorganization treatment.
entries.details: The assigned textbook reproduces selected judicial opinion passages; brief based only on those assigned extracts.
entries.facts: Mrs. Gregory owned United Mortgage Corp. (UMC), which held appreciated Monitor shares. To extract those shares with better shareholder tax treatment, she arranged formation of Averill, transferred Monitor stock in what looked like a divisive reorganization, received all Averill stock, then liquidated Averill about three days later and sold the Monitor stock. The Board initially respected literal compliance; Learned Hand's Second Circuit and the Supreme Court did not.
entries.issue: Could a brief, tax-driven corporate shell sequence qualify as a reorganization under the historical statute when its paper steps fulfilled all literal conditions?
entries.holding: No. Both courts held the plan lacked the corporate-reorganization character contemplated by Congress and was a device for a stock distribution rather than a genuine reorganization.
entries.reasoning: Learned Hand emphasized statutory meaning includes purpose and context, not individual words alone, while accepting taxpayers' right to lower tax where authorized. Supreme Court held the temporary company had no actual business/corporate purpose and its only function was to facilitate a preconceived stock transfer, so the literal form did not control.
entries.rule: A claimed tax-free corporate reorganization must fall within the statute's substantive purpose; a contrived, transitory entity and unrelated steps may fail even if formal conditions appear satisfied.
entries.exam: Separate motive from transaction's character; compare legitimate business restructuring with three-day shell; apply substance-over-form without claiming all tax planning is unlawful.
entries.examApplication: Separate motive from transaction's character; compare legitimate business restructuring with three-day shell; apply substance-over-form without claiming all tax planning is unlawful.
entries.examTrap: Tax reduction motive alone is NOT a disqualifier; the fatal deficiency was failure to accomplish a reorganization of the kind statute intended.
entries.source: Federal Income Taxation, 19th ed., assigned reproduced court opinion excerpt, Week 9 pp.416–419
entries.sourceRole: Opinion passages reproduced on assigned pages, not cited-only references

entries.title: Knetsch v. United States
entries.summary: No. The Supreme Court affirmed that the scheme did not create qualifying indebtedness, disallowing the deductions as a sham transaction.
entries.laymanExplanation: A taxpayer borrowed $4 million from an insurer to purchase that insurer's annuity bonds, then repeatedly borrowed back their rising value. The Court denied claimed interest deductions because no genuine debt/substance was created.
entries.details: The assigned textbook reproduces selected judicial opinion passages; brief based only on those assigned extracts.
entries.facts: Knetsch paid $4,000 in cash and signed $4 million of nonrecourse notes to acquire $4,004,000 of 30-year deferred annuity bonds from Sam Houston Life Insurance Company. Annuities earned 2.5% while notes charged 3.5%; he prepaid $140,000 plus $3,465 interest in 1953, then took $99,000 of further advances against the bonds. Similar borrow-back steps recurred in 1954 and 1955. When he surrendered bonds in 1956, policy loan balance nearly equaled cash value and he received only $1,000.
entries.issue: Were the purported interest payments on the insurer-financed annuity obligations deductible 'interest on indebtedness' under §163(a)?
entries.holding: No. The Supreme Court affirmed that the scheme did not create qualifying indebtedness, disallowing the deductions as a sham transaction.
entries.reasoning: Matching debt and annuity cash values plus automatic borrow-back left only a thin net interest cost and virtually no annuity value; most so-called interest was a round-trip rebate and remaining amount was a fee for tax deductions. The majority relied on Gregory, despite absence of earlier explicit statutory bar. Douglas's dissent emphasized real insurer contracts and preferred a legislative remedy.
entries.rule: Section 163 interest requires real indebtedness; tax labels and paperwork on economically offsetting transactions do not establish deductible loan interest when no meaningful nontax substance exists.
entries.exam: Calculate $4m×3.5%=$140k cost and $4m×2.5%=$100k tax-favored growth; compare tax deduction with pretax loss and examine §264 statutory restrictions.
entries.examApplication: Calculate $4m×3.5%=$140k cost and $4m×2.5%=$100k tax-favored growth; compare tax deduction with pretax loss and examine §264 statutory restrictions.
entries.examTrap: Do not conclude every tax-motivated annuity or loan is sham; the majority found little meaningful independent transaction and a nearly circular flow, while dissent disagreed.
entries.source: Federal Income Taxation, 19th ed., assigned reproduced court opinion excerpt, Week 9 pp.421–424

entries.title: Winn-Dixie Stores, Inc. v. Commissioner
entries.summary: No. Eleventh Circuit affirmed denial of policy-related interest and fee deductions because the transaction had no pretax economic substance or meaningful non-tax business purpose.
entries.laymanExplanation: A grocery chain insured more than 36,000 employees and borrowed against the policies to create huge tax interest deductions. The court rejected the program although an old insurance statute appeared to allow it.
entries.details: The assigned textbook reproduces selected judicial opinion passages; brief based only on those assigned extracts.
entries.facts: Winn-Dixie initiated a 1993 corporate-owned life insurance (COLI) program covering roughly 36,000 full-time employees, acting as sole beneficiary. The company borrowed against policy cash value at over 11%, with costs and fees exceeding pretax economic value; planners projected billions in tax savings over 60 years. Winn-Dixie exited as 1996 legislation threatened benefits. The tax court found no profit potential or business purpose and denied deductions.
entries.issue: Could Winn-Dixie rely on an express historical §264(a)(3) exception for life-insurance policy-loan interest to prevent a sham/economic-substance inquiry?
entries.holding: No. Eleventh Circuit affirmed denial of policy-related interest and fee deductions because the transaction had no pretax economic substance or meaningful non-tax business purpose.
entries.reasoning: Despite facial compliance with an insurance-code exception, Knetsch controlled; statutes permitting legitimate qualifying borrowing do not shield arrangements generating only tax savings. The district-level findings of no pretax profit and business purpose were undisputed on appeal.
entries.rule: Sham/economic-substance scrutiny can defeat a claimed deduction on artificial policy-loan arrangements despite literal compliance with a narrow interest-deduction exception.
entries.exam: Identify historical statutory exception, compare independent real borrowing and cash investment hypotheticals, find absence of actual profit potential and whether §7701(o) codification would now apply.
entries.examApplication: Identify historical statutory exception, compare independent real borrowing and cash investment hypotheticals, find absence of actual profit potential and whether §7701(o) codification would now apply.
entries.examTrap: Do not suggest all corporate-owned life insurance is abusive; the court targeted this broad scheme's economics and purpose.

entries.laymanExplanation: Even if work clothes were genuinely business-only, a normal employee usually cannot deduct unreimbursed work costs.
entries.legalExplanation: The textbook describes suspension of many miscellaneous itemized deductions for 2018–2025. Congress extended this restriction beyond 2025; distinguish deduction limitations from whether expenditure meets §162 for working-condition fringe purposes.

entries.legalExplanation: Employer-provided working condition fringe exclusion requires hypothetical deduction under §162/§167; §67(g) restrictions on employee itemized deductions do not generally defeat §132(d) hypothetical test. Separate reimbursement and substantiation rules may apply.

entries.title: Pevsner three-prong work-clothing test
entries.summary: Work clothing deductible only if required or essential, not adaptable to ordinary wear, and not actually worn as everyday clothing.
entries.laymanExplanation: A logo safety uniform might count. Expensive designer clothes still look like ordinary clothes even if you wear them only at work.
entries.legalExplanation: Fifth Circuit adopted objective standard: (1) specific employment requirement (or essential for self-employed), (2) not adaptable to ordinary street wear, (3) not in fact worn as ordinary wear. All prongs needed to deduct cost/maintenance when otherwise eligible.
entries.details: Fifth Circuit adopted objective standard: (1) specific employment requirement (or essential for self-employed), (2) not adaptable to ordinary street wear, (3) not in fact worn as ordinary wear. All prongs needed to deduct cost/maintenance when otherwise eligible.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation, 19th ed. (2023), assigned Week 9 Chapter 9 pp.448–450.
entries.elements: Required or essential for work; objectively NOT suitable for general wear; actually NOT so worn.
entries.examTrap: Objective adaptability—not taxpayer's taste, income or lifestyle—controls.

entries.title: Objective suitability for general wear
entries.summary: A garment's general use is judged by ordinary streetwear standards, not personal preferences.
entries.laymanExplanation: You may never wear your designer office dress to dinner, but others could. That is enough to fail suitability.
entries.legalExplanation: Pevsner reversed Tax Court's subjective approach because different taxpayers' lifestyles would yield unequal outcomes and hard-to-administer deductions.
entries.details: Pevsner reversed Tax Court's subjective approach because different taxpayers' lifestyles would yield unequal outcomes and hard-to-administer deductions.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation, 19th ed. (2023), assigned Week 9 Chapter 9 pp.448–450.

entries.title: Uniforms and protective gear versus business attire
entries.summary: Distinctive uniforms and protective garments can satisfy work-clothing rules; regular suits and fashionable designer garments generally cannot.
entries.laymanExplanation: A firefighter's protective coat has no normal personal function; a business suit does.
entries.legalExplanation: Some specialized protective clothing may meet all three Pevsner prongs. Clothing that can be worn ordinarily, even if 'uniform-like' or employer mandated, fails objective streetwear test.
entries.details: Some specialized protective clothing may meet all three Pevsner prongs. Clothing that can be worn ordinarily, even if 'uniform-like' or employer mandated, fails objective streetwear test.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation, 19th ed. (2023), assigned Week 9 Chapter 9 pp.447–451.

entries.title: Nondeductible clothing maintenance follows nondeductible clothing
entries.summary: Cleaning clothes that fail the work-clothing test generally does not create an independent business deduction.
entries.laymanExplanation: If a suit itself is personal clothing, dry-cleaning it usually stays personal.
entries.legalExplanation: Pevsner held the $240 clothing-maintenance cost nondeductible alongside $1,381.91 clothing cost.
entries.details: Pevsner held the $240 clothing-maintenance cost nondeductible alongside $1,381.91 clothing cost.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation, 19th ed. (2023), assigned Week 9 Chapter 9 pp.448–450.

entries.title: Pevsner v. Commissioner
entries.summary: No. Fifth Circuit reversed, rejecting the Tax Court's subjective taxpayer-lifestyle test and denying clothing and maintenance deductions.
entries.laymanExplanation: A luxury-boutique manager wore expensive designer outfits only at work, but they were still normal street clothes. She could not deduct their cost or cleaning.
entries.legalExplanation: Deduct work clothes only when (1) specifically required/essential at work; (2) not adaptable to general ordinary clothing use; and (3) not actually worn as ordinary clothes, plus ordinary Code limitations.
entries.details: Judicial opinion excerpt reproduced in the assigned casebook pages. Full case brief expands here.
entries.facts: Sandra Pevsner managed a Dallas Yves Saint Laurent boutique and was expected to wear that brand's clothing. She bought four blouses, three skirts, slacks, trench coat, sweaters, jackets, scarves, belts, shoes and jewelry. Her home/social life was modest, and she said she never wore these items outside work. She claimed $1,381.91 of apparel costs and $240 maintenance. Tax Court allowed both because she personally found the apparel unsuitable for her lifestyle.
entries.issue: Is work-required clothing deductible when it is objectively suitable as ordinary streetwear but the particular taxpayer would not personally wear it off duty?
entries.holding: No. Fifth Circuit reversed, rejecting the Tax Court's subjective taxpayer-lifestyle test and denying clothing and maintenance deductions.
entries.reasoning: Objective suitability ensures administrability and equal treatment. Employer requirement and nonuse off duty were undisputed; adaptable general streetwear failed the second prong regardless of price, personal taste or social class.
entries.rule: Deduct work clothes only when (1) specifically required/essential at work; (2) not adaptable to general ordinary clothing use; and (3) not actually worn as ordinary clothes, plus ordinary Code limitations.
entries.exam: Apply three prongs to fire protective gear, branded uniforms, high-end suits, ceremonial gowns, chef attire; note §67(g) separate employee-level restriction.
entries.examApplication: Apply three prongs to fire protective gear, branded uniforms, high-end suits, ceremonial gowns, chef attire; note §67(g) separate employee-level restriction.
entries.examTrap: Employer demand and actual work-only usage are insufficient if clothes are objectively usable for ordinary streetwear.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), reproduced opinion Pevsner v. Commissioner, assigned Week 9 pp.448–450
entries.sourceRole: Reproduced judicial opinion, not incidental citation

entries.title: §280A(a)/(c) residence expenses generally disallowed unless exception
entries.summary: Home expenses attributable to business use require satisfying a specific statutory exception.
entries.laymanExplanation: Checking work email on the couch doesn't give you a home-office deduction.
entries.legalExplanation: §280A(a) baseline denial; §280A(c)(1) provides exception for qualifying business space regularly and exclusively used as principal place of business, customer meeting site, or separate structure, with limitations and exceptions.
entries.details: §280A(a) baseline denial; §280A(c)(1) provides exception for qualifying business space regularly and exclusively used as principal place of business, customer meeting site, or separate structure, with limitations and exceptions.

entries.title: Regular and exclusive home-office use
entries.summary: A separately identified area must actually be used exclusively and on a regular basis for qualifying business purposes.
entries.laymanExplanation: Using the living room as a family lounge every night generally ruins the exclusive-use claim.
entries.legalExplanation: The Popov source emphasizes living room was filled only with practice/recording materials, child excluded, no one slept there, and 4–5 hours daily professional practice supported exclusive use.

entries.title: §280A(c)(1)(A) principal place of business
entries.summary: The home can be primary place of business even though clients or performance take place elsewhere, depending on relevant law and facts.
entries.laymanExplanation: A violinist may earn money at concert halls but do her most essential work practicing in a dedicated room at home.
entries.legalExplanation: Popov, under Soliman analysis, compared relative importance of professional tasks and time at each site, finding extensive exclusive home practice tipped balance. Later statutory administrative/management tests can also apply.
entries.details: Popov, under Soliman analysis, compared relative importance of professional tasks and time at each site, finding extensive exclusive home practice tipped balance. Later statutory administrative/management tests can also apply.

entries.title: Soliman two factors: relative importance and time at each site
entries.summary: Court weighed location of key professional functions plus time spent at home versus outside locations.
entries.laymanExplanation: Where you deliver services may matter, but hours doing essential preparation at home also matter.
entries.legalExplanation: Popov applied Commissioner v. Soliman (opinion discussed in excerpt, not reproduced): relative importance of professional activity (including weight to goods/services delivery) and comparative hours; time became decisive when relative importance inconclusive.
entries.details: Popov applied Commissioner v. Soliman (opinion discussed in excerpt, not reproduced): relative importance of professional activity (including weight to goods/services delivery) and comparative hours; time became decisive when relative importance inconclusive.

entries.title: Business-use percentage for home-office expenses
entries.summary: Allocate qualifying shared home costs by business area/share, subject to statutory limits.
entries.laymanExplanation: If 20% of the home's floor area is exclusively qualifying office space, part of rent and utility costs may be allocated.
entries.legalExplanation: Popov claimed 40% annual rent and 20% electricity, but appellate decision principally addressed entitlement to deduction; verify reasonableness and exact allocable amount separately.
entries.details: Popov claimed 40% annual rent and 20% electricity, but appellate decision principally addressed entitlement to deduction; verify reasonableness and exact allocable amount separately.

entries.title: Popov v. Commissioner
entries.summary: Yes. Ninth Circuit reversed Tax Court and held her dedicated practice space was her principal business location under then-governing analysis.
entries.laymanExplanation: A professional violinist spent four to five hours every day practicing in an exclusively used living-room studio; the appeals court allowed her home office deduction.
entries.legalExplanation: Under then-applicable Soliman comparative framework, principal place-of-business status turns on relative importance and time at sites; where functional importance is even, substantial exclusive work at home can decide. Apply later §280A amendments for current rules.
entries.details: Judicial opinion excerpt reproduced in the assigned casebook pages. Full case brief expands here.
entries.facts: Katia Popov performed with symphony orchestras and at many Hollywood studio recording sessions, sometimes receiving sheet music only when recording began. No employer provided practice space. In the family's one-bedroom Los Angeles apartment, living room contained recording equipment, sheet music and chair; daughter was barred and no one slept there. She practiced 4–5 hours daily. Deducted 40% rent and 20% electricity. Tax Court denied because earnings were from concerts/studios.
entries.issue: Was Popov's living room her principal place of business within §280A(c)(1)(A), despite paid performances occurring elsewhere?
entries.holding: Yes. Ninth Circuit reversed Tax Court and held her dedicated practice space was her principal business location under then-governing analysis.
entries.reasoning: Soliman first weighed relative importance of functions; essential home practice and outside performances were both central, and service-delivery frame inadequately captured music. Where importance was indecisive, time controlled: much more time practicing at home than recording/performing. Exclusive use existed.
entries.rule: Under then-applicable Soliman comparative framework, principal place-of-business status turns on relative importance and time at sites; where functional importance is even, substantial exclusive work at home can decide. Apply later §280A amendments for current rules.
entries.exam: Compare essential preparation, outside service delivery, comparative hours and exclusive use. Evaluate current statute's administrative/management alternative separately.
entries.examApplication: Compare essential preparation, outside service delivery, comparative hours and exclusive use. Evaluate current statute's administrative/management alternative separately.
entries.examTrap: The decision is not a blanket right for every person who works remotely; it analyzes 1993 facts under pre-1997 statutory framework.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), reproduced opinion Popov v. Commissioner, assigned Week 9 pp.451–455
entries.sourceRole: Reproduced judicial opinion, not incidental citation

entries.title: §280A(d)(1) vacation residence personal-use threshold

entries.laymanExplanation: Rent 100 days: 10%=10; threshold is 14. Personal use of 15 days exceeds threshold.
entries.legalExplanation: Apply greater-of rule and distinguish more-than threshold from equal-to threshold; dwelling unit deemed used as residence if personal-use days exceed amount. Other family/related-party use may count as personal use.

entries.title: Vacation home rental/personal allocation
entries.summary: Costs attributable to rental use may be prorated between rental and personal use.
entries.laymanExplanation: If you rented for half the total use days, only appropriate shares of mixed bills enter the rental computation.
entries.legalExplanation: §280A(e) calls for pro-rata allocation of specified expenses. For dwelling treated as residence, §280A(c)(5) limits net rental deductions to qualified rental income after allocable interest/taxes and other statutory costs.

entries.summary: For personal-use vacation residence, allowable rental expenses generally cannot create a taxable rental loss under §280A.
entries.laymanExplanation: You can't use your personal beach home's rental operation to erase salary income by claiming unlimited expenses.
entries.legalExplanation: If personal use exceeds the residence threshold and rental period ≥15 days, rental deductions (other than specified otherwise allowable interest/taxes) limited to rental revenue after related allocations; disallowed losses may carry under applicable rules.

entries.title: Smith — childcare treated as personal rather than deductible §162 expense
entries.summary: Hiring caregivers so both spouses can work does not, by itself, convert childcare into a business deduction.
entries.laymanExplanation: The babysitter lets you go to work, but the tax court treated care of children as family expense.
entries.legalExplanation: Smith v. Commissioner (1939) rejected a 'but for childcare, wife couldn't work' theory; childcare relates to the family regardless of occupational activity. The casebook flags dated assumptions about working women; Congress later created separate benefits.

entries.summary: Being unable to work without incurring a cost is not sufficient to prove the cost is business rather than personal.
entries.laymanExplanation: If you couldn't work without childcare, food or clothing, that doesn't make every expense deductible.

entries.title: Smith v. Commissioner
entries.citation: 40 B.T.A. 1038 (1939), aff’d without opinion, 113 F.2d 114 (2d Cir. 1940)
entries.summary: No. Board denied deduction; Second Circuit affirmed without opinion.
entries.laymanExplanation: Both parents worked and paid a nanny, but the tax board called childcare a personal family expense rather than a deductible cost of earning wages.
entries.legalExplanation: Childcare costs are ordinarily personal under §262 rather than §162 business expenses even when work requires childcare; statutory §§21/129 may independently provide tax benefits.
entries.details: Judicial opinion excerpt reproduced in the assigned casebook pages. Full case brief expands here.
entries.facts: Married couple both worked for income and hired nursemaids to care for their infant child so wife could work away from home. They claimed caregiver wages as business expenses and argued that without those wages wife could not earn taxable income.
entries.issue: Is a working family's childcare expense a deductible ordinary and necessary trade/business cost under §162's predecessor rather than nondeductible personal §262 expense?
entries.holding: No. Board denied deduction; Second Circuit affirmed without opinion.
entries.reasoning: Direct connection to earning compensation was insufficient because similar but-for logic could turn food, medicine, shelter and clothes into business costs. Caring for children arose from family needs regardless of employment. The opinion reflected antiquated assumptions about women and unpaid household work; later Congress created separate credits/exclusions.
entries.rule: Childcare costs are ordinarily personal under §262 rather than §162 business expenses even when work requires childcare; statutory §§21/129 may independently provide tax benefits.
entries.exam: Distinguish employment-caused outlays from business-origin expense; identify why §21 credit/§129 exclusion, not §162, governs modern benefits.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish employment-caused outlays from business-origin expense; identify why §21 credit/§129 exclusion, not §162, governs modern benefits.
entries.examTrap: The dated gender and domestic-role reasoning is not an element of current law; legal result concerns §162/262 classification.

entries.title: Reg. §1.162-5: education maintaining or improving current job skills
entries.summary: Education may be deductible if maintaining/improving skills in existing work, but not if qualifying for new occupation or meeting initial job requirements.

Separate employee §67(g) limitations may disallow expenses otherwise §162-deductible.
entries.details: Reg. §1.162-5(a) allows maintaining/improving current business skills or employer/legal required continuation education; §1.162-5(b) bars minimum-qualification and new-trade/business education regardless of helpfulness. Separate employee §67(g) limitations may disallow expenses otherwise §162-deductible.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), assigned Week 10 Chapter 9 pp.463–468
entries.elements: Current trade/business; skills maintained/improved or existing-position requirement; NOT initial minimum education; NOT qualification for new trade; apply separate §67(g) deduction restrictions.

entries.title: New trade or business qualification disqualifier
entries.summary: An education program qualifying taxpayer for a substantially different profession is not deductible under §162 even if current job benefits.
entries.laymanExplanation: A detective going to law school gets qualified as a lawyer, a different trade.
entries.legalExplanation: Compare tasks taxpayer legally/professionally could perform before versus after program; credential that first qualifies for new trade bars §162 deduction.
entries.details: Compare tasks taxpayer legally/professionally could perform before versus after program; credential that first qualifies for new trade bars §162 deduction.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), assigned Week 10 Chapter 9 pp.464–467

entries.title: Minimum educational requirements disqualifier
entries.summary: Education needed first to qualify for a current profession cannot be deducted as maintaining existing skills.
entries.laymanExplanation: A new accountant can't deduct a required first certification course by claiming it helps work.
entries.legalExplanation: Reg. §1.162-5(b)(2) bars qualification for new trade and (b)(1) minimum educational requirements. Later professional courses are treated separately depending on job connection and statutory limitations.
entries.details: Reg. §1.162-5(b)(2) bars qualification for new trade and (b)(1) minimum educational requirements. Later professional courses are treated separately depending on job connection and statutory limitations.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), assigned Week 10 Chapter 9 pp.465–467

entries.title: Carroll — general college courses unrelated to detective's required skills
entries.summary: General liberal-arts study was insufficiently connected to taxpayer's existing detective duties for §162 expense.
entries.laymanExplanation: A detective's philosophy, English and history courses may improve general knowledge but not closely enough his policing skills.
entries.legalExplanation: Carroll v. Commissioner held $720.80 college tuition nondeductible; broad betterment wasn't enough, even though police encouraged attendance and taxpayer contemplated law school.
entries.details: Carroll v. Commissioner held $720.80 college tuition nondeductible; broad betterment wasn't enough, even though police encouraged attendance and taxpayer contemplated law school.

entries.title: Kopaigora — existing-job EMBA can qualify despite temporary unemployment
entries.summary: Education improving established finance-management skills can be deductible if not qualifying for new occupation.
entries.laymanExplanation: An experienced hotel controller's EMBA reinforced his existing management work, not a brand-new career.
entries.legalExplanation: Kopaigora held $18,879 EMBA deduction allowable under historical §162 rules because management/finance skills existed pre-degree; temporary unemployment with active job search did not terminate trade/business. For 2026, separate §67(g) limits ordinary employees.
entries.details: Kopaigora held $18,879 EMBA deduction allowable under historical §162 rules because management/finance skills existed pre-degree; temporary unemployment with active job search did not terminate trade/business. For 2026, separate §67(g) limits ordinary employees.

entries.title: §127 employer educational assistance exclusion
entries.summary: Qualifying employer educational program may exclude assistance up to combined annual amount.
entries.laymanExplanation: Your employer may cover qualified tuition or student loans tax-free up to the cap.
entries.legalExplanation: Book lists $5,250 per year and describes student-loan assistance as expiring after 2025; P.L.119-21 made qualified loan payments permanently eligible; amount $5,250 in 2026, adjusted for inflation after 2026.
entries.details: Book lists $5,250 per year and describes student-loan assistance as expiring after 2025; P.L.119-21 made qualified loan payments permanently eligible; amount $5,250 in 2026, adjusted for inflation after 2026.

entries.title: Other education benefits — §§117, 25A, 221, 529, 530
entries.summary: Separate statutory exclusions, credits, loan-interest deductions and savings-plan benefits subsidize education.
entries.laymanExplanation: Even when tuition isn't a business deduction, scholarship and education-credit rules may help.

entries.title: General job search versus targeted business-acquisition costs
entries.summary: General search for a new business generally personal; costs of specific attempted acquisition may be capitalized/recoverable.
entries.laymanExplanation: Looking around for businesses to buy is different from paying legal fees for one specific target deal.
entries.legalExplanation: Rev. Rul. 77-254 (cited in notes) distinguishes preliminary general search from targeted acquisition and failed transaction costs; §195 may be relevant for specific business start-up expenses.
entries.details: Rev. Rul. 77-254 (cited in notes) distinguishes preliminary general search from targeted acquisition and failed transaction costs; §195 may be relevant for specific business start-up expenses.

entries.title: Carroll v. Commissioner
entries.summary: No. Seventh Circuit affirmed denial of tuition deduction.
entries.laymanExplanation: A detective took English, philosophy, history and political science in college; the court said general knowledge wasn't close enough to his existing detective job to deduct tuition.
entries.legalExplanation: Job-skill education must maintain or improve specific skills required in present employment; general college education useful to everyone is normally personal and not deductible under §162.
entries.details: Judicial opinion excerpt reproduced in the assigned casebook pages. Full case brief expands here.
entries.facts: Chicago police detective James Carroll enrolled at DePaul University in preparation for law school, majoring in philosophy and taking two English, two philosophy, one history and one political science courses. Claimed $720.80 on 1964 return. Police order encouraged college education and accommodated scheduling; he argued courses improved his detective skills.
entries.issue: Were general college courses deductible education expenses because they generally help a practicing detective perform better?
entries.holding: No. Seventh Circuit affirmed denial of tuition deduction.
entries.reasoning: Reg. §1.162-5 demands sufficient concrete connection between education and skills required in taxpayer's existing job, not just general improvement or value of a degree; general courses were not shown closely related to particular police duties.
entries.rule: Job-skill education must maintain or improve specific skills required in present employment; general college education useful to everyone is normally personal and not deductible under §162.
entries.exam: Compare general liberal arts with courses directly related to police duties; separately apply new-trade rule to planned law-school qualification.
entries.examApplication: Compare general liberal arts with courses directly related to police duties; separately apply new-trade rule to planned law-school qualification.
entries.examTrap: An employer's encouragement of school is not proof that coursework satisfies §1.162-5.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), reproduced opinion Carroll v. Commissioner, assigned Week 10 pp.463–464
entries.sourceRole: Reproduced judicial opinion, not incidental citation

entries.title: Kopaigora v. Commissioner
entries.summary: No. Tax Court Summary Opinion allowed tuition as a business education expense under historical rules.
entries.laymanExplanation: A longtime corporate financial manager earned an EMBA to improve existing leadership and accounting skills; even losing his job while in school didn't destroy the original business connection.
entries.legalExplanation: Education maintaining/improving established job skills can qualify for §162 when it does not meet initial requirements or qualify taxpayer for a new trade; active search can preserve business continuity through temporary unemployment.
entries.details: Judicial opinion excerpt reproduced in the assigned casebook pages. Full case brief expands here.
entries.facts: Marriott senior assistant controller and accountant worked managing hotel accounts, budgets and teams. Enrolled in BYU Executive MBA July 2010 while employed, commuting to school every other weekend. Job terminated without justification April 2011, but he continued program and actively sought finance jobs. Hired soon after graduation in substantially similar VP-finance role. Claimed $18,879 EMBA expenses.
entries.issue: Did EMBA qualify petitioner for new trade or interrupt his existing profession during unemployment, defeating §162 education deduction?
entries.holding: No. Tax Court Summary Opinion allowed tuition as a business education expense under historical rules.
entries.reasoning: Before degree he was already established in finance/management; coursework improved pertinent skills rather than opening materially new occupational tasks. Temporary unemployment coupled with active search in same field preserved trade/business, and later job did not require degree.
entries.rule: Education maintaining/improving established job skills can qualify for §162 when it does not meet initial requirements or qualify taxpayer for a new trade; active search can preserve business continuity through temporary unemployment.
entries.exam: Compare skills/duties before and after degree, new license/qualification, temporary unemployment and employer demands. Add current §67(g) restriction for ordinary employee deduction.
entries.examApplication: Compare skills/duties before and after degree, new license/qualification, temporary unemployment and employer demands. Add current §67(g) restriction for ordinary employee deduction.
entries.examTrap: The opinion decides whether education met §162 criteria under historical years; it does not make such unreimbursed employee costs deductible in 2026.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), reproduced opinion Kopaigora v. Commissioner, assigned Week 10 pp.465–467
entries.sourceRole: Reproduced judicial opinion, not incidental citation

legalWarning.label: §67(g) LIMITS 2026 DEDUCTIONS
legalWarning.reason: The opinion allowed a 2011 unreimbursed employee deduction. Most miscellaneous itemized employee business deductions are disallowed in tax year 2026; subject-matter §162 classification remains instructive.

entries.title: Personal commuting generally nondeductible under §§162 and 262
entries.summary: Routine trips between home and regular workplace are generally treated as personal choices.
entries.laymanExplanation: Driving from your home to your office is normally not deductible—even if you need to get to work.
entries.legalExplanation: Flowers treats costs due to where taxpayer chose to live as personal; IRS Rev. Rul. 99-7 offers distinct daily transportation exceptions for temporary work sites or qualifying home principal business location.
entries.details: Flowers treats costs due to where taxpayer chose to live as personal; IRS Rev. Rul. 99-7 offers distinct daily transportation exceptions for temporary work sites or qualifying home principal business location.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), assigned Week 10 Chapter 9 pp.469–484

entries.title: Flowers three conditions for away-from-home business travel
entries.summary: Travel deduction requires reasonable/necessary travel, away from tax home, and business exigencies.
entries.laymanExplanation: Your employer requiring you to stay somewhere else temporarily can be business travel; choosing to live far from your job is not.
entries.legalExplanation: Supreme Court held lawyer's Jackson–Mobile travel arose from his wish to keep Jackson family home while railroad's principal office was Mobile. Three conditions are expenses reasonable/necessary, away from home, and directly required by the business, not personal preference.
entries.details: Supreme Court held lawyer's Jackson–Mobile travel arose from his wish to keep Jackson family home while railroad's principal office was Mobile. Three conditions are expenses reasonable/necessary, away from home, and directly required by the business, not personal preference.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), assigned Week 10 Chapter 9 pp.470–473
entries.elements: (1) Reasonable and necessary travel expense; (2) incurred while away from home; (3) directly required by employer's or taxpayer's business (business exigencies).

entries.title: Tax home for §162(a)(2)
entries.summary: Business tax home generally centered on main business/work location rather than family residence for travel deductions.
entries.laymanExplanation: You may live in one city and work in another, but tax law often treats the job location as your tax home.
entries.legalExplanation: The Flowers majority did not settle every possible definition of home, but its business-exigencies requirement denies travel motivated solely by living arrangements. Hantzis examines work-home nexus, not just address.
entries.details: The Flowers majority did not settle every possible definition of home, but its business-exigencies requirement denies travel motivated solely by living arrangements. Hantzis examines work-home nexus, not just address.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), assigned Week 10 Chapter 9 pp.471–481

entries.title: Temporary versus indefinite employment away from home
entries.summary: Temporary assignment in another work locality may permit duplicative living/travel costs where business, not personal preference, creates the duplication.
entries.laymanExplanation: A short transfer to another city may count; taking a permanent job there and keeping your old home usually doesn't.
entries.legalExplanation: Hantzis reasons expenses must be business-required duplicate costs from a continuing business base; assignment duration alone does not give a student/worker a separate tax home. Statutory §162(a) limits indefinite assignments and year-long expectations.
entries.details: Hantzis reasons expenses must be business-required duplicate costs from a continuing business base; assignment duration alone does not give a student/worker a separate tax home. Statutory §162(a) limits indefinite assignments and year-long expectations.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), assigned Week 10 Chapter 9 pp.477–481

entries.title: Hantzis — job away from personal home without prior local work nexus
entries.summary: Travel/lodging to temporary new-job city was denied when taxpayer had no business activity at residence city.
entries.laymanExplanation: A Harvard law student working in NYC while her spouse remained in Boston couldn't deduct NYC living costs just because she planned to return to Boston.
entries.legalExplanation: Hantzis v. Commissioner rejected deduction for summer legal-assistant work in NYC; she had no current trade/business job base in Boston, so maintaining Boston personal home was not business-related duplication.
entries.details: Hantzis v. Commissioner rejected deduction for summer legal-assistant work in NYC; she had no current trade/business job base in Boston, so maintaining Boston personal home was not business-related duplication.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), assigned Week 10 Chapter 9 pp.477–482

entries.title: Rev. Rul. 99-7 — daily transportation exceptions
entries.summary: Temporary location outside regular metro area, temporary location with another regular worksite, or home principal business site can make daily transportation deductible.
entries.laymanExplanation: Driving from your qualifying home office to a client job site may count even when regular home-to-office travel doesn't.
entries.legalExplanation: Ruling enumerates (a) temporary worksite outside taxpayer's metro area; (b) temporary worksite with one or more other regular work sites; (c) home is principal place of business and destination in same business. Each requires statutory/regulatory factual qualifications.
entries.details: Ruling enumerates (a) temporary worksite outside taxpayer's metro area; (b) temporary worksite with one or more other regular work sites; (c) home is principal place of business and destination in same business. Each requires statutory/regulatory factual qualifications.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), assigned Week 10 Chapter 9 pp.482

entries.title: Commuting-disallowance fairness
entries.summary: Transportation expenses are unavoidable for many, but reflect housing and work-market constraints.
entries.laymanExplanation: A low-income housekeeper or traveling construction worker has less freedom to choose residence than a well-paid suburban lawyer.
entries.legalExplanation: The assigned nine-scenario problem contrasts family choices, employer provision, mobility, public transit and disparate treatment; policy background, NOT an exception unless a rule applies.
entries.details: The assigned nine-scenario problem contrasts family choices, employer provision, mobility, public transit and disparate treatment; policy background, NOT an exception unless a rule applies.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), assigned Week 10 Chapter 9 pp.482–484

entries.title: Commissioner v. Flowers
entries.summary: No. Supreme Court reversed appellate court and upheld the IRS's disallowance.
entries.laymanExplanation: The railroad's lawyer lived in Jackson by choice, although his employer's main office was in Mobile. Traveling between home and main office was personal commuting, not deductible business travel.
entries.legalExplanation: Deductible travel must be reasonable, incurred while away from tax home, AND necessitated by business rather than personal choice of residence.
entries.details: Judicial opinion excerpt reproduced on syllabus-assigned pages.
entries.facts: Railroad counsel John Flowers had long established family/home and political life in Jackson, Mississippi. Employer's main office and his business post were in Mobile, Alabama. He negotiated permission to retain Jackson residence at own expense, making 33 trips in 1939 and 40 in 1940. In those years claimed $900 and $1,620 for Jackson–Mobile travel and Mobile meals/hotels despite employer not requiring that living arrangement.
entries.issue: Are travel and double-living expenses deductible as incurred 'while away from home in pursuit of trade or business' where they follow employee's personal decision to live away from principal post?
entries.holding: No. Supreme Court reversed appellate court and upheld the IRS's disallowance.
entries.reasoning: §162(a)(2) requires travel expense reasonable/necessary, away from home, and business exigencies directly necessitating the expense. Court avoided resolving every possible 'home' definition because third factor failed: railroad's work was in Mobile, Jackson residence was taxpayer's personal preference. Rutledge dissented, favoring plain sense of family home.
entries.rule: Deductible travel must be reasonable, incurred while away from tax home, AND necessitated by business rather than personal choice of residence.
entries.exam: Spot employee's business headquarters vs family domicile, who requires travel and whether expenses duplicate living costs because of job requirements.
entries.examApplication: Spot employee's business headquarters vs family domicile, who requires travel and whether expenses duplicate living costs because of job requirements.
entries.examTrap: The Court did not definitively settle all possible tax-home definitions; its decision rested on lack of business exigency.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., reproduced Commissioner v. Flowers excerpt, assigned Week 10 pp.469–473

entries.title: Hantzis v. Commissioner
entries.summary: No. First Circuit reversed Tax Court allowance and denied §162(a)(2) travel costs.
entries.laymanExplanation: A Harvard law student took temporary New York legal work while maintaining a Boston apartment with her husband. Because she had no work base in Boston, her NYC costs weren't away-from-business-home expenses.
entries.legalExplanation: To deduct duplicative living expenses while temporarily away, taxpayer generally needs a business-linked tax home whose retention (not simply family residence) is required by business; temp job alone cannot manufacture it.
entries.details: Judicial opinion excerpt reproduced on syllabus-assigned pages.
entries.facts: Harvard law student Catharine Hantzis lived with husband in Cambridge/Boston; took 10-week summer legal-assistant job at New York firm in 1975 after failing to find Boston work. Spent $3,204 on transport, meals and NYC lodging while earning $3,750. They claimed deduction for cost of living away from Boston; she had no parallel summer job or business activity in Boston.
entries.issue: Are temporary work-city lodging and transportation deductible when the taxpayer's only business/work site is the temporary city and the maintained residence is personal?
entries.holding: No. First Circuit reversed Tax Court allowance and denied §162(a)(2) travel costs.
entries.reasoning: Although taxpayer did work in a trade/business and temporary nature alone was not decisive, duplicated costs lacked business exigency because no business reason required a Boston tax home. Boston was where spouse lived, not continuing location of work. Contrasts a taxpayer dispatched from an existing work base for temporary distant assignment.
entries.rule: To deduct duplicative living expenses while temporarily away, taxpayer generally needs a business-linked tax home whose retention (not simply family residence) is required by business; temp job alone cannot manufacture it.
entries.exam: Test simultaneous/ongoing work connection to principal home, temporary versus indefinite job, competing business exigency; distinguish Flowers and worker temporarily transferred from original business base.
entries.examApplication: Test simultaneous/ongoing work connection to principal home, temporary versus indefinite job, competing business exigency; distinguish Flowers and worker temporarily transferred from original business base.
entries.examTrap: Hantzis did not establish that no temporary travel is deductible; tax home and business reason for preserving it were decisive.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., reproduced Hantzis v. Commissioner excerpt, assigned Week 10 pp.477–482

entries.summary: Work-required travel away from tax home can support transportation, meals and lodging subject to separate §274 restrictions.

entries.laymanExplanation: If the work meeting is genuine but the trip is mostly vacation, airfare may not qualify in the same way.

entries.title: Rudolph — Supreme Court dismissal, no merits majority ruling
entries.summary: The Court dismissed certiorari as improvidently granted; separately excerpted Harlan/Douglas reasoning contrasts compensation and business travel.
entries.laymanExplanation: The insurance salesman won a New York trip, but the Justices disagreed about whether it was a taxable bonus or business travel.
entries.legalExplanation: Rudolph v. United States, 370 U.S. 269 (1962), per curiam DIG. Harlan separately defended tax on reward and denial of deduction; Douglas dissented, treating employer-paid trip as business-related and spouses' participation useful. No Supreme Court majority merits holding establishing either view.
entries.details: Rudolph v. United States, 370 U.S. 269 (1962), per curiam DIG. Harlan separately defended tax on reward and denial of deduction; Douglas dissented, treating employer-paid trip as business-related and spouses' participation useful. No Supreme Court majority merits holding establishing either view.

entries.examTrap: Do NOT treat Justice Harlan's separate opinion or Douglas's dissent as the Supreme Court majority's binding merits decision.

entries.title: Employer-paid travel and §132 working condition fringe
entries.summary: Employer travel benefit may be excluded if employee would have a hypothetical business-expense deduction.
entries.laymanExplanation: Free vacation reward is generally taxable compensation; a genuine work trip can be different.
entries.legalExplanation: Since §132 enactment in 1984, assess if employee-paid version would be deductible under §162, apart from general §67(g) employee deduction suspension; §274 and spousal travel restrictions still matter.
entries.details: Since §132 enactment in 1984, assess if employee-paid version would be deductible under §162, apart from general §67(g) employee deduction suspension; §274 and spousal travel restrictions still matter.

entries.title: Rudolph v. United States (DIG; separate opinions)
entries.summary: Supreme Court dismissed certiorari as improvidently granted, leaving lower-court tax determination undisturbed; NO Supreme Court merits majority holding on inclusion or business deduction.
entries.laymanExplanation: An insurance salesman earned an employer-paid New York convention/vacation. The Supreme Court dismissed the case without a majority merits ruling; excerpts debate whether it was compensation or work travel.
entries.legalExplanation: A DIG does not establish binding Supreme Court merits rule; under modern §132(d), employer-provided work benefit generally excluded if hypothetically §162-deductible, subject to personal-purpose and §274 limits.
entries.details: Judicial opinion excerpt reproduced on syllabus-assigned pages.
entries.facts: Southland Life Insurance paid $560 allocable travel/convention expenses for salesman Rudolph and wife to travel from Dallas to New York with 150 employees/officers and 141 wives, because he met sales quota. Company included meetings/luncheons but much sightseeing/recreation; taxpayer claimed excluded business travel or deductible expense; lower courts viewed it as sales reward/vacation.
entries.issue: Did employer trip value constitute §61 compensation, and were convention meals/travel/lodging deductible or excludable as business expense/fringe?
entries.holding: Supreme Court dismissed certiorari as improvidently granted, leaving lower-court tax determination undisturbed; NO Supreme Court merits majority holding on inclusion or business deduction.
entries.reasoning: Per curiam dismissal. Harlan separate opinion reasoned employer's purpose was bonus/reward and taxpayers' purpose primarily pleasure, so income and no §162 deduction. Douglas's dissent (joined by Black) argued the employer convened agents for business and spouses helped the company's relationships, so no taxable compensation for genuine reimbursed travel and/or deductions. Modern §132(d) governs hypothetical deduction test.
entries.rule: A DIG does not establish binding Supreme Court merits rule; under modern §132(d), employer-provided work benefit generally excluded if hypothetically §162-deductible, subject to personal-purpose and §274 limits.
entries.exam: Precisely identify procedural posture; analyze separate Harlan and Douglas views, business motive evidence, optional attendance, quota bonus, spouse's business role and modern §132.
entries.examApplication: Precisely identify procedural posture; analyze separate Harlan and Douglas views, business motive evidence, optional attendance, quota bonus, spouse's business role and modern §132.
entries.examTrap: NEVER cite Harlan separate opinion as majority holding or claim Rudolph was affirmed on the merits.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., reproduced Rudolph v. United States (DIG; separate opinions) excerpt, assigned Week 10 pp.485–489

legalWarning.label: NO SUPREME COURT MERITS HOLDING
legalWarning.reason: The Court DISMISSED certiorari as improvidently granted; Harlan and Douglas passages are separate opinions. §132(d), enacted later, controls modern working-condition-fringe analysis.
