entries.title: Moss — routine daily law-firm lunches generally personal
entries.summary: Daily same-law-firm lunches at a normal preferred cafe lacked necessary incremental business meal cost.
entries.laymanExplanation: Discussing cases while eating lunch doesn't necessarily turn lunch into a deduction.
entries.legalExplanation: Judge Posner in Moss held daily Cafe Angelo lunch costs personal under §§162/262 even though firm had real work discussions and meetings were convenient. Contrast bona fide client entertainment or meals exceeding ordinary personal consumption, subject to current §274.
entries.details: Judge Posner in Moss held daily Cafe Angelo lunch costs personal under §§162/262 even though firm had real work discussions and meetings were convenient. Contrast bona fide client entertainment or meals exceeding ordinary personal consumption, subject to current §274.

entries.title: Client/business-contact meals versus daily coworker lunches
entries.summary: Meals genuinely used for business relationship-building can differ from usual routine lunches.
entries.laymanExplanation: Taking a paying client to an expensive restaurant for business can be different from your everyday lunch.
entries.legalExplanation: Moss reasons outside clients reduce negotiation friction, costs may exceed ordinary meals, while work meetings among colleagues at same restaurant daily often do not; fact-specific nature and frequency matter.
entries.details: Moss reasons outside clients reduce negotiation friction, costs may exceed ordinary meals, while work meetings among colleagues at same restaurant daily often do not; fact-specific nature and frequency matter.

entries.title: Moss v. Commissioner
entries.summary: No. Seventh Circuit affirmed Tax Court's disallowance of the partners' everyday lunch expense.
entries.laymanExplanation: Law-firm partners ate lunch in the same restaurant almost every day to coordinate hundreds of cases. Their regular lunch still counted as personal spending, even while talking business.
entries.legalExplanation: Ordinary personal meals do not become business expenses merely because business is discussed while eating; genuinely qualifying client or other business meals may differ, then §274(n) generally limits deduction.
entries.details: Judicial opinion excerpt reproduced on syllabus-assigned pages.
entries.facts: Moss and other partners of a Chicago insurance-defense trial firm each handled hundreds of cases. Because time was limited, they ate at Cafe Angelo almost every working day for business discussions, settlements and courtroom assignment planning. Claimed about $1,000 per year each in ordinary meal cost. The partners liked the restaurant and did not establish any increased meal cost due to business use.
entries.issue: Does conducting necessary firm business discussions over a convenient daily lunch make the everyday meal cost a deductible §162 business expense?
entries.holding: No. Seventh Circuit affirmed Tax Court's disallowance of the partners' everyday lunch expense.
entries.reasoning: Food is personal consumption even when convenience of conversation helps business. Client/business-contact meals may cost more than ordinary eating and reduce friction, but law-firm members still needed to eat and the daily meal was at their preferred cafe. No incremental cost or allocation for meeting space proved; court emphasized frequency, circumstances and distinction between meeting and the food itself.
entries.rule: Ordinary personal meals do not become business expenses merely because business is discussed while eating; genuinely qualifying client or other business meals may differ, then §274(n) generally limits deduction.
entries.exam: Separate meeting value from personal food, insider/outsider, incremental cost, frequency and specific evidence of business purpose; then apply §274 50% cap only if expense otherwise deductible.
entries.examApplication: Separate meeting value from personal food, insider/outsider, incremental cost, frequency and specific evidence of business purpose; then apply §274 50% cap only if expense otherwise deductible.
entries.examTrap: The 50% meal limit doesn't make half of all coworker lunches automatically deductible.

entries.summary: Legal costs classified as business/investment or personal by the origin and nature of underlying claim, not consequences to income/assets.
entries.laymanExplanation: A divorce lawsuit about controlling shares is still a personal divorce claim, even if losing could cost you your business.

entries.legalExplanation: Gilmore rejected 'if I lose I'll lose salary and investments' logic; otherwise almost every personal liability threatening a taxpayer's assets could be relabeled an investment-conservation cost.

entries.legalExplanation: Gilmore discusses Kornhauser v. United States as contrast; no separately reproduced Kornhauser opinion appears in assigned pages.

entries.title: Title-defense legal fees may be capitalized into property basis
entries.summary: A later Gilmore district-court decision allowed capitalization of attorneys’ fees genuinely incurred to defend title; that is a different issue from deducting legal fees currently.
entries.laymanExplanation: A divorce lawyer’s bill may not reduce this year's income, but fees actually protecting ownership of stock may instead increase the stock's tax cost. Defending an unrelated personal debt is different.
entries.legalExplanation: The assigned Notes and Questions, pp.499–500, describe the later decision Gilmore v. United States, 245 F. Supp. 383 (N.D. Cal. 1965): the district court accepted basis capitalization for qualifying title-defense expenses notwithstanding the marital origin of the dispute. The court distinguished personal litigation expenses that were not in fact primarily incurred to defend title. This is a related decision described in the notes, NOT part of the reproduced Supreme Court holding or a separate assigned opinion brief. The notes ask whether costs of defending a personal-debt lawsuit against a lien on the taxpayer's house could likewise be capitalized; the question remains intentionally unsolved.

entries.title: United States v. Gilmore
entries.summary: No. Supreme Court reversed the Court of Claims and held the contested legal expenses nondeductible as personal marital-origin litigation.
entries.laymanExplanation: A businessman spent over $40,000 defending divorce claims that might have cost him his controlling GM dealership stock. Supreme Court denied deduction because the lawsuit originated in marriage, not his business.
entries.legalExplanation: Origin and nature of underlying legal claim, not financial consequences of adverse ruling or subjective motive to protect investments, determines business/investment versus personal legal-expense character.
entries.details: Judicial opinion excerpt reproduced on syllabus-assigned pages.
entries.facts: Husband owned controlling stock in three General Motors dealerships, earning roughly $66,800 salary plus $83,000 dividends annually. Wife brought contentious divorce with California community-property claims, arguing marriage-related profits and stock were marital assets; failure could threaten his control and franchise/salary. Husband won and paid $40,611.36 in legal expenses. Court of Claims allowed ~80% because of threat to income stock; IRS disputed under §212/§262.
entries.issue: Are legal fees paid to defeat spouse's community-property divorce claims deductible as cost of conservation of income-producing property under §212(2) because losing might jeopardize taxpayer's business?
entries.holding: No. Supreme Court reversed the Court of Claims and held the contested legal expenses nondeductible as personal marital-origin litigation.
entries.reasoning: §212 expanded income-producing categories but retained §162-origin/business-personal divide. Character derives from 'origin and character of claim'—here marital relationship—rather than consequences to property/business if lost. Else almost any personal lawsuit jeopardizing wealth could be reclassified as property conservation. Contrasted former partnership-fee disputes in Kornhauser.
entries.rule: Origin and nature of underlying legal claim, not financial consequences of adverse ruling or subjective motive to protect investments, determines business/investment versus personal legal-expense character.
entries.exam: Ask what activity/property relationship gave rise to lawsuit; differentiate former partner fee dispute, divorce/community property, and direct title litigation; then apply §§162/212/262 and any separate modern restrictions.
entries.examApplication: Ask what activity/property relationship gave rise to lawsuit; differentiate former partner fee dispute, divorce/community property, and direct title litigation; then apply §§162/212/262 and any separate modern restrictions.
entries.examTrap: The fact losing marital litigation would destroy income/stock ownership is NOT sufficient for a business deduction.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., reproduced United States v. Gilmore excerpt, assigned Week 10 pp.495–499

entries.legalExplanation: Ability to pay is a tax policy justification for some personal deductions; it is not a blanket deduction rule absent statutory authorization.

entries.legalExplanation: Deductions lower the tax base, not the tax dollar-for-dollar. Thus high-bracket taxpayers generally gain more, subject to limits and eligibility; critics contrast flat or refundable credits.

entries.title: Ochs — boarding school to aid sick spouse generally nondeductible
entries.summary: Sending children to boarding school to reduce stress on recovering spouse was treated as family expense rather than medical treatment.
entries.laymanExplanation: Keeping kids away helped a sick mother recover, but the majority said tuition and boarding were still a family cost.
entries.legalExplanation: The majority distinguished medical treatment from household services lost or reallocated because of illness, despite doctor's medical advice. Frank dissented, reasoning a strictly physician-prescribed incremental cost devoted to health recovery should qualify.

entries.title: But-for causation versus medical-purpose classification
entries.summary: Without illness a cost might not occur, but that causal fact does not settle whether the payment buys medical care.
entries.laymanExplanation: An illness can explain why you hire help; it doesn't always change what you bought.
entries.legalExplanation: Notes after Ochs compare causation in Ochs/Taylor and emphasize that ordinary personal consumption may be intertwined with medically useful spending.

entries.title: Incremental cost to accommodate medical needs
entries.summary: Some rulings allow cost above ordinary consumption when a disability creates directly tailored additional expense.
entries.laymanExplanation: A Braille book costing more than the ordinary edition may produce a deduction for only the price difference.
entries.legalExplanation: The notes reference Braille materials, school mobility aid, and qualifying equipment or home accessibility changes where extra cost serves distinct disability or medical treatment purpose; specific rules govern.

entries.title: Medical capital improvements — incremental qualifying portion
entries.summary: Qualifying home adaptations for medical needs may be deductible only to extent cost exceeds any home value increase.
entries.laymanExplanation: Installing a medically necessary elevator can count to extent it doesn't simply add value to the house.
entries.legalExplanation: Reg. §1.213-1(e)(1)(iii) permits qualifying capital medical expenditures reduced by associated increase in property value; need a medical purpose and documentation.

entries.title: Prescribed clarinet as medical therapy
entries.summary: A nontraditional item can qualify if medically necessary and narrowly tailored to an actual condition.
entries.laymanExplanation: A child with a jaw problem may have prescribed clarinet lessons; the qualifying instrument and lessons may count even though musical lessons are normally personal.
entries.legalExplanation: Rev. Rul. 62-210 approved limited-cost clarinet plus necessary lessons to alleviate diagnosed malocclusion. This is IRS guidance in notes, not a reproduced judicial opinion.

topics.description: Distinguish medical treatment from personal and family consumption; two assigned opinions

entries.title: §213(d)(9) cosmetic surgery exclusion and exceptions
entries.summary: Primarily appearance-enhancing procedures generally excluded unless treating disease, improving bodily function, or qualifying disfigurement/deformity.
entries.laymanExplanation: A purely cosmetic nose job is usually personal, but reconstruction after an accident may qualify.
entries.legalExplanation: Statute excludes cosmetic surgery directed at appearance without meaningful functional/disease benefit, with exception for qualifying congenital abnormality, accident/trauma or disfiguring disease.
entries.details: Statute excludes cosmetic surgery directed at appearance without meaningful functional/disease benefit, with exception for qualifying congenital abnormality, accident/trauma or disfiguring disease.

entries.title: Private letter ruling (PLR) — nonprecedential taxpayer-specific guidance
entries.summary: IRS written response to identified taxpayer facts generally binds only that requester, not all taxpayers.
entries.laymanExplanation: A PLR tells one taxpayer the IRS's view; you cannot treat it like a court decision everyone may cite as precedent.
entries.legalExplanation: Section 6110(k)(3) restricts precedential use; practitioners may consult published PLRs as indications of IRS reasoning, not as binding authority.

entries.title: PLR 202114001 — costs of surrogacy/IVF involving third parties
entries.summary: IRS allowed taxpayer-linked sperm donation/freezing but denied surrogacy, third-party egg retrieval, childbirth and related legal/agency fees on stated facts.
entries.laymanExplanation: The couple could deduct their own direct medical procedures, but IRS said most expenses for the egg donor and surrogate were not medical care of the taxpayers.
entries.legalExplanation: The 2021 PLR applied §213(d)'s treatment/structure/function wording to two spouses and third parties, citing Magdalin, Longino and Morrissey as authorities. It did not identify disease treated in requesting spouses; medically related costs imposed on unrelated third parties were excluded.

entries.title: Medical scope of assisted reproductive technology
entries.summary: Care of the taxpayer/spouse/dependent may qualify; costs for other persons and purely elective preservation raise harder questions.
entries.laymanExplanation: IVF may qualify under certain conditions, but that does not make every donor or surrogate expense automatically deductible.
entries.legalExplanation: Casebook distinguishes medical interventions affecting an eligible person's body from third-party procedures. Its notes explicitly leave elective egg freezing and some ART outcomes unresolved; do not invent bright-line rules.

entries.summary: Tax Court allowed gender-affirming hormone and surgery costs as qualifying medical care on taxpayer's diagnosis; IRS acquiesced historically.
entries.laymanExplanation: The chapter says gender-related medical care was allowed under §213 for that taxpayer.
entries.legalExplanation: The text references O'Donnabhain v. Commissioner, 134 T.C. 34 (2010), with IRS acquiescence; the opinion itself is not reproduced in this assigned pages, so this stays contextual.

entries.summary: The book quotes IRS Publication 502 on costs of legal abortions; application involves time- and jurisdiction-specific law.
entries.laymanExplanation: The chapter discusses legal abortions as medical costs and flags post-Dobbs legal complexity.
entries.legalExplanation: Textbook states a then-existing IRS position and notes uncertainty about legality after Dobbs. Treat as sourced historical discussion; for any actual taxpayer question examine current law/jurisdiction, not a universal legal conclusion.

entries.title: Elective egg freezing — unresolved §213 classification
entries.summary: The text asks whether preserving eggs without diagnosed inability to conceive is deductible and expressly leaves the question open.
entries.laymanExplanation: Choosing to freeze eggs for the future isn't automatically the same as medical treatment of infertility.
entries.legalExplanation: IRS Pub. 502 recognizes some IVF and temporary egg/sperm storage to overcome inability to have children, but elective storage before infertility is described as uncertain in the assigned material.

topics.title: C. Medical Boundaries, Reproductive Care & PLR
topics.description: Cosmetic procedures, assisted reproduction, PLR 202114001, third-party medical care, and policy
topics.assignmentSource: Fall 2026 Federal Income Taxation syllabus: Week 11, Chapter 10 pp.510–516

entries.title: §170 charitable contribution deduction
entries.summary: Qualifying gift to eligible government or exempt organization can reduce taxable income, subject to amount, recipient, type, documentation, and annual ceilings.
entries.laymanExplanation: Donating to a recognized charity may lower your taxable income; handing money to a friend doesn't.
entries.legalExplanation: §170(a)(1), §170(c) establish eligible contributions and donees. Generally itemized, with separate nonitemizer cash allowance beginning 2026. Check percentage of contribution base, type of property, private benefit, valuation and substantiation.
entries.details: §170(a)(1), §170(c) establish eligible contributions and donees. Generally itemized, with separate nonitemizer cash allowance beginning 2026. Check percentage of contribution base, type of property, private benefit, valuation and substantiation.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), assigned Week 11 Chapter 10 pp.516–517
entries.elements: (1) Eligible donor; (2) qualifying donee; (3) voluntary gift rather than purchase; (4) correct contribution amount/character; (5) applicable AGI limits/floor; (6) substantiation.

entries.title: Eligible donee — §170(c)
entries.summary: U.S. government, qualifying educational, religious, scientific or charitable organizations and other enumerated recipients.
entries.laymanExplanation: Donations generally must go to organizations the tax law recognizes, not just to any needy person.
entries.legalExplanation: Section 170(c) covers public entities and qualifying organizations organized and operated for authorized purposes, with noninurement and lobbying/political campaign requirements.
entries.details: Section 170(c) covers public entities and qualifying organizations organized and operated for authorized purposes, with noninurement and lobbying/political campaign requirements.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), assigned Week 11 Chapter 10 pp.516–517

entries.title: §501(c)(3) qualified nonprofit
entries.summary: Organization organized/operated exclusively for specified exempt purposes, no private inurement and limits on lobbying/political intervention.
entries.laymanExplanation: A charitable nonprofit can have an exemption from its own income tax and may receive deductible donations.
entries.legalExplanation: Exempt entity under §501(c)(3) differs from §170(c) deductibility eligibility; most major charities overlap, but qualification, public charity/private foundation distinction, and UBIT remain relevant.
entries.details: Exempt entity under §501(c)(3) differs from §170(c) deductibility eligibility; most major charities overlap, but qualification, public charity/private foundation distinction, and UBIT remain relevant.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), assigned Week 11 Chapter 10 pp.517, 527–528

entries.title: §170 AGI percentage ceilings and carryforward
entries.summary: 2023 textbook describes 60% contribution-base limit on cash to public charities, lower 30%/20% limits for certain gifts and entities, and five-year carryover.
entries.laymanExplanation: If you donate too much for the annual limit, you may have to wait to deduct the excess in later years.
entries.legalExplanation: The applicable §170(b) annual ceiling varies by cash/property character and donee; excess usually eligible for five-year carryover, subject to additional limitations. Casebook treats some corporate cap as 10%. Starting 2026 §170 adds a 0.5% AGI floor for itemizers and a 1% corporate-income floor while retaining general 10% corporate ceiling.
entries.details: The applicable §170(b) annual ceiling varies by cash/property character and donee; excess usually eligible for five-year carryover, subject to additional limitations. Casebook treats some corporate cap as 10%. Starting 2026 §170 adds a 0.5% AGI floor for itemizers and a 1% corporate-income floor while retaining general 10% corporate ceiling.

legalWarning.label: 2026 CHARITY FLOORS
legalWarning.reason: Starting 2026, itemizers generally face a new 0.5% of contribution-base floor for charitable gifts; corporate donors a 1% floor subject to statutory exceptions and carryforward rules.

entries.title: 2026 nonitemizer cash donation deduction — §170(p)
entries.summary: Eligible nonitemizers can deduct up to $1,000 single or $2,000 joint in qualifying cash donations for 2026.
entries.laymanExplanation: Even if you take the standard deduction, you may still subtract some cash gifts separately.
entries.legalExplanation: The source footnote mentions a limited allowance but does not provide 2026 figures. Under 2025 legislation, §170(p) is operative for 2026: eligible cash donations to qualified organizations are deductible subject to $1,000/$2,000 limits. This is a current-law annotation, not silently imported into historical chapter.
entries.details: The source footnote mentions a limited allowance but does not provide 2026 figures. legalWarning.label: 2026 NONITEMIZER RULE
legalWarning.reason: 2026 tax returns permit a cash charitable deduction up to $1,000 ($2,000 joint) for eligible nonitemizers, separately from Schedule A.

entries.title: Appreciated long-term capital-gain property gift
entries.summary: Qualifying long-term capital-gain property given directly to a public charity can generally be deducted at FMV rather than original basis, subject to limits.
entries.laymanExplanation: Donating stock that rose from $10,000 to $1 million can avoid selling and recognizing the gain while permitting a large charitable deduction.
entries.legalExplanation: The textbook's example contrasts selling appreciated shares then donating cash with gifting shares directly. §170(e) usually allows fair market value for long-term capital gain property, subject to percentage limits, related-use, qualified appraisals and exceptions.
entries.details: The textbook's example contrasts selling appreciated shares then donating cash with gifting shares directly. §170(e) usually allows fair market value for long-term capital gain property, subject to percentage limits, related-use, qualified appraisals and exceptions.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), assigned Week 11 Chapter 10 pp.517–518
entries.examTrap: The FMV deduction does not apply automatically to inventory, short-term gain property, certain private-foundation gifts or unrelated-use tangible property.

entries.title: Basis-limited charitable property deduction
entries.summary: For property that would generate ordinary income or short-term capital gain upon sale, allowable deduction generally reduced to basis.
entries.laymanExplanation: Giving property you have owned briefly generally cannot create a deduction for appreciation you haven't paid tax on.
entries.legalExplanation: Section 170(e)(1) reduces contribution amount for gain that would not be long-term capital gain in the hypothetical sale. Also applies to certain tangible personal property if charity's intended use unrelated to exempt mission.
entries.details: Section 170(e)(1) reduces contribution amount for gain that would not be long-term capital gain in the hypothetical sale. Also applies to certain tangible personal property if charity's intended use unrelated to exempt mission.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), assigned Week 11 Chapter 10 pp.517–518

entries.title: Tangible personal property's related-use limitation — §170(e)(1)(B)
entries.summary: Art gift to museum for exhibition may qualify at FMV; identical work sold by unrelated-use donee can be basis-limited.
entries.laymanExplanation: A painting displayed by an art museum is different from a painting a hospital immediately sells.
entries.legalExplanation: For appreciated tangible personal property, recipient organization's use related to its exempt purpose controls whether special FMV treatment remains available; separate disposition and recapture rules also relevant.
entries.details: For appreciated tangible personal property, recipient organization's use related to its exempt purpose controls whether special FMV treatment remains available; separate disposition and recapture rules also relevant.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), assigned Week 11 Chapter 10 pp.518

entries.title: Five-year charitable contribution carryover
entries.summary: Certain otherwise eligible donations exceeding current annual limit may be deducted in a later year.
entries.laymanExplanation: If a gift is above your annual cap, it might count in the next five tax years.
entries.legalExplanation: Section 170(d) carries over specified excess gifts subject to time, category, ordering and tax-year limits; not every unrelated disallowance can be carried forward.
entries.details: Section 170(d) carries over specified excess gifts subject to time, category, ordering and tax-year limits; not every unrelated disallowance can be carried forward.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), assigned Week 11 Chapter 10 pp.517

entries.title: Deductions versus credits for charitable giving
entries.summary: An income-tax deduction is worth more per dollar to higher tax brackets; a specified credit could equalize subsidies.
entries.laymanExplanation: At a 37% rate $100 deducted may save $37; a 20% credit would be $20 for either taxpayer.
entries.legalExplanation: Book compares U.S. marginal-rate-based subsidy with Canada's two-tier donation credit (historical example 17% on first $250 and 29% above). This is policy context, not current Canadian tax-rate advice.
entries.details: Book compares U.S. marginal-rate-based subsidy with Canada's two-tier donation credit (historical example 17% on first $250 and 29% above). This is policy context, not current Canadian tax-rate advice.

entries.title: Charitable tax expenditure and donor control
entries.summary: A charity deduction subsidizes organizations chosen by private donors instead of public budgeting.
entries.laymanExplanation: A portion of tax revenue goes toward donor-selected charities rather than government-selected spending.
entries.legalExplanation: Source notes potential higher giving, taxpayer distribution differences and democratic accountability concerns; amount and direction of subsidy are policy questions rather than separate legal elements.

topics.title: D. Charitable Deduction — §170 Mechanics
topics.description: Eligible organizations, AGI ceilings, cash versus appreciated property, equity implications

entries.title: Quid pro quo gift: subtract fair value of goods/services received
entries.summary: If the charity gives donor something of value in return, deduction generally limited to payment minus FMV of benefit.
entries.laymanExplanation: Donate $100 and get a $20 tote bag: generally an $80 gift.
entries.legalExplanation: Regulations and §170 require truly donative portion; value to donor generally measured by fair market value of benefits, not the charity's internal cost. Special de minimis and membership rules may apply.
entries.details: Regulations and §170 require truly donative portion; value to donor generally measured by fair market value of benefits, not the charity's internal cost. Special de minimis and membership rules may apply.

entries.title: Ottawa Silica substantial private business benefit can defeat gift
entries.summary: Donation of land for public high school did not produce deductible charitable contribution when expected new public roads substantially benefited donor's adjoining parcels.
entries.laymanExplanation: Company gave school land but benefited because roads made its other land much more valuable; court treated it as a business deal.
entries.legalExplanation: Federal Circuit affirmed denial under substantial benefit/quid pro quo test where benefits exceeded those generally enjoyed by public. Fact that district initially requested the gift did not determine its nature.
entries.details: Federal Circuit affirmed denial under substantial benefit/quid pro quo test where benefits exceeded those generally enjoyed by public. Fact that district initially requested the gift did not determine its nature.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), assigned Week 11 Chapter 10 pp.520–524
entries.examTrap: A charitable recipient's public purpose doesn't settle donor's entitlement when donor receives a substantial private return.

entries.title: Dominant donative intent versus objectively substantial benefit
entries.summary: Courts can examine both donor's intent and benefits expected to determine whether transfer is gift or economic exchange.
entries.laymanExplanation: You can't call something a donation and ignore the private deal you expected in return.
entries.legalExplanation: Notes contrast Ottawa Silica's substantial benefit analysis with DuVal's inquiry into taxpayer's primary/dominant intent backed by objective circumstances. DuVal is cited-only, not reproduced.
entries.details: Notes contrast Ottawa Silica's substantial benefit analysis with DuVal's inquiry into taxpayer's primary/dominant intent backed by objective circumstances. DuVal is cited-only, not reproduced.

entries.title: §6115 written disclosure for quid pro quo gifts over $75
entries.summary: Charity must give good-faith estimate of goods/services received for donor payments above statutory threshold.
entries.laymanExplanation: If you donate $100 for dinner worth $35, charity must identify that benefit and you ordinarily can deduct only the charitable portion.
entries.legalExplanation: Section 6115 requires specified disclosure for quid pro quo contributions exceeding $75, but amounts under $75 still remain subject to fair-value subtraction where donor receives a nontrivial benefit.
entries.details: Section 6115 requires specified disclosure for quid pro quo contributions exceeding $75, but amounts under $75 still remain subject to fair-value subtraction where donor receives a nontrivial benefit.

entries.title: Psychic benefits and naming recognition
entries.summary: Naming rights or general public recognition often are not valued as quid pro quo goods/services for basic charitable deduction.
entries.laymanExplanation: Having your name on a building may be rewarding but isn't usually treated like buying a $20 tote bag.
entries.legalExplanation: Source distinguishes tangible/identifiable goods and services from less measurable psychic returns in the baseline charitable deduction discussion.
entries.details: Source distinguishes tangible/identifiable goods and services from less measurable psychic returns in the baseline charitable deduction discussion.

entries.title: College athletic seating rights — §170(l)
entries.summary: Payments giving donor rights to buy college sports tickets are not charitable contributions under special statutory rule.
entries.laymanExplanation: Paying the university just to get priority seats isn't a deductible gift.
entries.legalExplanation: The textbook highlights §170(l) denying deduction when payment buys rights to college athletic-event seating; investigate exact statutory language when applied.

entries.title: §170(f)(8) contemporaneous written acknowledgment and property valuation documentation
entries.summary: Substantial gifts require written recipient acknowledgment; noncash gifts can require detailed descriptions and qualified appraisal.
entries.laymanExplanation: Keep the receipt and proper appraisal—claiming your damaged vase is worth $50,000 won't make it true.
entries.legalExplanation: Book notes >$250 gift acknowledgment, >$500 noncash information, >$5,000 property appraisal categories and exemptions; taxpayers must meet governing current forms, timing and valuation standards. Isbell shows court reduced inflated antique jar value to $800.

entries.title: Isbell jar valuation — cited-only example
entries.summary: Taxpayer raised claimed jar deduction from $15,000 to $50,000; IRS valued it at $800 despite auction price $360.
entries.laymanExplanation: Calling an old cracked jar a priceless antique wasn't supported by qualified expertise.
entries.legalExplanation: Textbook discusses Isbell v. Commissioner, 44 T.C.M. 1143 (1982), to illustrate valuation failures, but does not reproduce the judicial opinion. Court used expert government's $800 valuation.

entries.title: Religious service payments and exchange analysis
entries.summary: Payments for identifiable religious training services can be nondeductible quid pro quo, despite recipient's exempt status.
entries.laymanExplanation: Membership donations can qualify, but paying a set fee for a required service may not be a gift.
entries.legalExplanation: Book references Hernandez v. Commissioner (1989), which denied deductions for fixed-price Scientology auditing/training, later reporting a separate settlement. Hernandez is discussed, not a reproduced opinion; do not imply the settlement overruled the Supreme Court.

entries.title: Charitable contribution requires donative character
entries.summary: Court denied tax deduction for a court-ordered school-fund payment made as condition of avoiding imprisonment.
entries.laymanExplanation: Paying $145,000 because a judge demands it isn't charitable giving merely because a school receives it.
entries.legalExplanation: The casebook describes Lombardo v. Commissioner as cited example of lack of voluntariness/charitable impulse; the opinion itself is not reproduced.

entries.title: §501(c)(3) exemption: organized and operated for qualifying purposes
entries.summary: Entity may avoid income tax on mission-related receipts if organized and operated for enumerated exempt purposes and free of prohibited private inurement.
entries.laymanExplanation: Being a nonprofit doesn't automatically mean everything it earns is tax-free.
entries.legalExplanation: §501(c)(3) requires qualified organizational/operational purposes, no earnings inuring to private interests, and statutory lobbying/political campaign restrictions; §170 donor deductibility overlaps but differs.

entries.elements: Qualifying purpose; operated consistently with purpose; no private inurement; comply with lobbying/political campaign restrictions; public policy limits where applicable.

entries.title: Unrelated business income tax (UBIT) — §§511–514
entries.summary: Tax-exempt organization can owe tax on income from regularly carried-on activities not substantially related to its charitable purpose.
entries.laymanExplanation: A university might be exempt for education yet pay tax on an unrelated commercial business.
entries.legalExplanation: Casebook states organization-level tax exemption does not extend to unrelated activities; analyze §§511–514 and exceptions separately.

entries.title: Private foundation — §509
entries.summary: Qualifying §501(c)(3) entity with concentrated funding/control rather than broad public support, subject to additional rules.
entries.laymanExplanation: A wealthy family's foundation is a charity but typically faces stricter limits and annual payout requirements.
entries.legalExplanation: Book describes foundations funded principally by founders; §509 public charity/private-foundation classification carries §4941 self-dealing and §4942 payout duties and different donor percentage ceilings.
entries.details: Book describes foundations funded principally by founders; §509 public charity/private-foundation classification carries §4941 self-dealing and §4942 payout duties and different donor percentage ceilings.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), assigned Week 11 Chapter 10 pp.528

entries.title: Private foundation 5% distribution requirement and self-dealing rules
entries.summary: Private foundations generally must make qualifying annual distributions and avoid specified insider self-dealing.
entries.laymanExplanation: A family foundation can't simply stockpile assets forever or use them for its founders' private deals.
entries.legalExplanation: Section 4942 generally imposes minimum distributable amounts linked to adjusted assets; §4941 regulates self-dealing with disqualified persons. Source simplification 'at least 5%' omits adjustments/exceptions.
entries.details: Section 4942 generally imposes minimum distributable amounts linked to adjusted assets; §4941 regulates self-dealing with disqualified persons. Source simplification 'at least 5%' omits adjustments/exceptions.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), assigned Week 11 Chapter 10 pp.528

entries.title: §501(c)(3) political campaign/lobbying limits
entries.summary: Excess lobbying or partisan campaign intervention can jeopardize exemption or deductibility; non-501(c)(3) entities follow different rules.
entries.laymanExplanation: A charity can educate but generally can't run a candidate's campaign under its tax exemption.
entries.legalExplanation: Sections 501(c)(3), 170(c)(2)(D), 501(h) and §527 distinguish lobbying limits, campaign intervention, permissible issue advocacy and political organizations; apply specific activity tests.
entries.details: Sections 501(c)(3), 170(c)(2)(D), 501(h) and §527 distinguish lobbying limits, campaign intervention, permissible issue advocacy and political organizations; apply specific activity tests.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), assigned Week 11 Chapter 10 pp.528

entries.title: Bob Jones — fundamental public-policy limit on charitable exemption
entries.summary: Private school that practices racial discrimination inconsistent with fundamental public policy cannot qualify for §501(c)(3) exemption.
entries.laymanExplanation: Being a school or sincerely religious doesn't make a racially discriminatory policy eligible for public tax subsidy.
entries.legalExplanation: Supreme Court read common-law charitable purpose and established public policy into §§170 and 501(c)(3); racial discrimination in private education violated fundamental national policy. Court held government interest outweighed asserted religious burden on stated record.
entries.details: Supreme Court read common-law charitable purpose and established public policy into §§170 and 501(c)(3); racial discrimination in private education violated fundamental national policy. Court held government interest outweighed asserted religious burden on stated record.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), assigned Week 11 Chapter 10 pp.528–535
entries.examTrap: Bob Jones is a still-cited Supreme Court precedent; textbook's speculation about future change is NOT a holding that it was overturned.

entries.title: Bob Jones — IRS administrative interpretation and congressional response
entries.summary: Court found IRS interpretation supported by statute/charitable history and pointed to Congress's subsequent actions as approval.
entries.laymanExplanation: The IRS changed its position and the Court considered Congress's reaction in deciding it was authorized.
entries.legalExplanation: Bob Jones's majority reasoned congressional acquiescence and §501(i) reinforced IRS public-policy position; concurrence/dissent disputed the breadth and authority of judicial/agency expansion.
entries.details: Bob Jones's majority reasoned congressional acquiescence and §501(i) reinforced IRS public-policy position; concurrence/dissent disputed the breadth and authority of judicial/agency expansion.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), assigned Week 11 Chapter 10 pp.531–535

entries.title: Religious liberty and tax exemption in Bob Jones
entries.summary: Majority rejected Free Exercise challenge as applied to racially discriminatory private schools given overriding government interest.
entries.laymanExplanation: The schools claimed sincere beliefs, but the Court ruled tax benefits could be denied to discriminatory schools.
entries.legalExplanation: The opinion reserved questions about purely religious institutions; Powell and Rehnquist criticized the majority's theory to different degrees. The casebook poses modern doctrinal questions without resolving them.
entries.details: The opinion reserved questions about purely religious institutions; Powell and Rehnquist criticized the majority's theory to different degrees. The casebook poses modern doctrinal questions without resolving them.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), assigned Week 11 Chapter 10 pp.533–538

entries.title: Powell concurrence and Rehnquist dissent — competing approaches
entries.summary: Powell worried broad public-benefit standard threatened nonprofit diversity; Rehnquist disputed court/IRS authority absent statute.
entries.laymanExplanation: Even Justices agreeing discrimination was wrong disagreed on who may create the tax-exemption restriction.
entries.legalExplanation: In Bob Jones, Powell joined judgment but urged legislative clarity and pluralism; Rehnquist dissented on express statutory text/separation of powers, not because he endorsed racial discrimination.
entries.details: In Bob Jones, Powell joined judgment but urged legislative clarity and pluralism; Rehnquist dissented on express statutory text/separation of powers, not because he endorsed racial discrimination.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), assigned Week 11 Chapter 10 pp.534–535

entries.title: Private inurement
entries.summary: Charitable organization's net earnings cannot flow to insiders as impermissible private gain.
entries.laymanExplanation: A charity can't secretly funnel its surplus to directors or founders.
entries.legalExplanation: Section 501(c)(3) noninurement restriction; distinguish insider benefits from incidental reasonable compensation and from broader private benefit. The excerpt compares later private fundraising arrangements.
entries.details: Section 501(c)(3) noninurement restriction; distinguish insider benefits from incidental reasonable compensation and from broader private benefit. The excerpt compares later private fundraising arrangements.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), assigned Week 11 Chapter 10 pp.539

entries.title: Private benefit versus private inurement
entries.summary: A charity may jeopardize exemption by serving private interests too substantially, even if recipients not formal insiders.
entries.laymanExplanation: Giving one commercial fundraiser too good a deal can raise tax-exempt status concerns.
entries.legalExplanation: United Cancer Council case discussed as example, but not a reproduced opinion; appellate court rejected one insider framing yet remanded to consider duty of care and substantial private benefit.
entries.details: United Cancer Council case discussed as example, but not a reproduced opinion; appellate court rejected one insider framing yet remanded to consider duty of care and substantial private benefit.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), assigned Week 11 Chapter 10 pp.539

entries.title: United Cancer Council — cited charitable governance case
entries.summary: Charity raised nearly $30 million through solicitations but netted under $3 million while fundraisers earned about $8 million.
entries.laymanExplanation: A huge fundraising campaign can be a red flag if the charity barely benefits.
entries.legalExplanation: The casebook describes 165 F.3d 1173 (7th Cir. 1999) and subsequent settlement; it is contextual authority, not a reproduced assigned opinion. Distinguish private benefit from forbidden insider inurement.
entries.details: The casebook describes 165 F.3d 1173 (7th Cir. 1999) and subsequent settlement; it is contextual authority, not a reproduced assigned opinion. Distinguish private benefit from forbidden insider inurement.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), assigned Week 11 Chapter 10 pp.539

topics.description: 501(c)(3), private foundations, UBIT, public policy, private inurement
topics.assignmentSource: Fall 2026 Federal Income Taxation syllabus: Week 11, Chapter 10 pp.527–539

entries.title: Interest — price of borrowing money
entries.summary: Payment for use of money over time.
entries.laymanExplanation: You pay a lender for getting money today instead of waiting.
entries.legalExplanation: Code differentiates business, investment, qualified residence and disallowed consumer interest; classification depends on traced use of borrowed funds.
entries.details: Code differentiates business, investment, qualified residence and disallowed consumer interest; classification depends on traced use of borrowed funds.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 12 Chapter 10 pp.539–540

entries.title: §163(h) personal interest generally not deductible
entries.summary: Most borrowing to finance personal consumption yields nondeductible interest, unlike qualifying trade/business, investment or mortgage interest.
entries.laymanExplanation: Credit-card interest and interest on a vacation loan generally won't reduce your taxable income.
entries.legalExplanation: Section 163(h)(1) disallows personal interest with enumerated exceptions; qualified residence interest and education-loan interest have separate conditions/limits.
entries.details: Section 163(h)(1) disallows personal interest with enumerated exceptions; qualified residence interest and education-loan interest have separate conditions/limits.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 12 Chapter 10 pp.539–540

entries.title: Acquisition indebtedness — qualified residence interest
entries.summary: Secured borrowing used to buy, build or substantially improve qualified residence.
entries.laymanExplanation: Only mortgage debt used for the house's acquisition or major improvements usually counts; simply using the house as collateral isn't enough.
entries.legalExplanation: §163(h)(3) and related regulations define qualifying acquisition indebtedness, limited by eligible loan principal and number/type of residences; loan use and security both necessary.
entries.details: §163(h)(3) and related regulations define qualifying acquisition indebtedness, limited by eligible loan principal and number/type of residences; loan use and security both necessary.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 12 Chapter 10 pp.539–541

entries.title: Qualified home mortgage interest limit — §163(h)(3)
entries.summary: Generally interest on up to $750,000 qualifying acquisition debt for post-Dec.15,2017 indebtedness, with $1m grandfathering for many older mortgages.
entries.laymanExplanation: A $1 million new mortgage doesn't necessarily make all its interest deductible.
entries.legalExplanation: Casebook describes $750k cap; footnote predicts that pre-2018 $1m ceiling would disappear after 2025. IRS Publication 936 (2025) retains separate $1m pre-2017 grandfather rule. Verify year-specific thresholds; never treat book's future prediction as current law.
entries.details: Casebook describes $750k cap; footnote predicts that pre-2018 $1m ceiling would disappear after 2025. IRS Publication 936 (2025) retains separate $1m pre-2017 grandfather rule. Verify year-specific thresholds; never treat book's future prediction as current law.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 12 Chapter 10 pp.539–540

legalWarning.label: OLDER MORTGAGE GRANDFATHERING
legalWarning.reason: The book predicts a 2026 change to old-mortgage debt limits. Later IRS Publication 936 maintains the $1 million limit for qualifying pre-Dec.16,2017 debt, while newer qualifying debt generally uses $750,000.

entries.title: Mortgage Examples A/B/C: borrowed to purchase vs replenish cash vs leisure
entries.summary: Purchase with mortgage may qualify; home-secured loan taken after cash purchase or for leisure generally doesn't.
entries.laymanExplanation: Buying the house with borrowed money is different from borrowing against a fully paid home for a vacation.
entries.legalExplanation: Book's Example A: house $1.2m, down $200k, loan $1m, acquisition interest capped at $750k under new-loan assumptions. Example B: all cash then $1m loan to replace savings, no acquisition debt on stated facts. Example C: later $1m secured loan for travel/cars, no acquisition debt.
entries.details: Book's Example A: house $1.2m, down $200k, loan $1m, acquisition interest capped at $750k under new-loan assumptions. Example B: all cash then $1m loan to replace savings, no acquisition debt on stated facts. Example C: later $1m secured loan for travel/cars, no acquisition debt.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 12 Chapter 10 pp.540

entries.title: Imputed rent from owner-occupied home
entries.summary: Estimated rental value of living in one's own home, not included in current individual gross income.
entries.laymanExplanation: Homeowners 'pay rent to themselves' economically, but aren't taxed on that value.
entries.legalExplanation: Source compares exclusion of owner-occupied imputed rent plus mortgage interest deduction as housing subsidy; this is tax-policy concept, not a dollar deduction.
entries.details: Source compares exclusion of owner-occupied imputed rent plus mortgage interest deduction as housing subsidy; this is tax-policy concept, not a dollar deduction.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 12 Chapter 10 pp.540–541

entries.title: Interest income/consumer interest expense asymmetry
entries.summary: Interest earned on savings generally taxable even while personal loan interest nondeductible.
entries.laymanExplanation: Earn $10,000 interest but pay $10,000 on a personal loan? Your taxable interest can still be $10,000.
entries.legalExplanation: Book contrasts consumption-tax theory with current income tax's asymmetric treatment and discusses deferral of consumption.
entries.details: Book contrasts consumption-tax theory with current income tax's asymmetric treatment and discusses deferral of consumption.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 12 Chapter 10 pp.541

entries.title: Reg. §1.163-8T tracing: interest follows use of proceeds
entries.summary: Determine loan interest character from where borrowed money was actually spent, not what secured the loan.
entries.laymanExplanation: Borrow against your store to buy a boat: that's still personal-loan interest.
entries.legalExplanation: Treas. Reg. §1.163-8T(c) traces borrowed funds to expenditures. Mixed borrowed/nonborrowed funds may require allocation; labels or collateral alone do not establish business purpose.
entries.details: Treas. Reg. §1.163-8T(c) traces borrowed funds to expenditures. Mixed borrowed/nonborrowed funds may require allocation; labels or collateral alone do not establish business purpose.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 12 Chapter 10 pp.542–543
entries.examTrap: Collateral type and subjective borrowing plan are not the same as traced use of proceeds.

entries.title: Fungibility of money and tracing arbitrage
entries.summary: Cash can be routed so same economic situation creates different loan-use classifications under formal tracing rules.
entries.laymanExplanation: With $10k savings and $10k loan, paying for business with loan and vacation with cash can differ from the opposite order.
entries.legalExplanation: The textbook criticizes how fungibility rewards deliberate routing of money, requiring detailed regulatory tracing despite underlying similar economic position.
entries.details: The textbook criticizes how fungibility rewards deliberate routing of money, requiring detailed regulatory tracing despite underlying similar economic position.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 12 Chapter 10 pp.542–543

entries.title: §221 student loan interest deduction
entries.summary: Qualifying education loan interest eligible for above-the-line deduction up to $2,500 subject to MAGI phaseout and eligibility.
entries.laymanExplanation: You may subtract some interest paid on eligible student loans even if you don't itemize.
entries.legalExplanation: Section 221 provides up to $2,500 qualified interest deduction, with inflation-adjusted MAGI phaseouts and additional statutory conditions. Textbook's $85k single/$175k joint cutoff is 2022 historical, not 2026.
entries.details: Section 221 provides up to $2,500 qualified interest deduction, with inflation-adjusted MAGI phaseouts and additional statutory conditions. Textbook's $85k single/$175k joint cutoff is 2022 historical, not 2026.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 12 Chapter 10 pp.543

legalWarning.label: 2022 STUDENT LOAN THRESHOLDS
legalWarning.reason: Source phaseout MAGI thresholds were 2022 values. Compute 2026 with actual current phaseout, filing status and qualifying loans.

entries.title: Mortgage deduction subsidy and reform tradeoffs
entries.summary: Subsidizing interest may promote ownership but can raise housing prices and disproportionately benefit higher-income owners.
entries.laymanExplanation: Tax breaks can help some homeowners yet increase purchase prices for others.
entries.legalExplanation: Source asks whether homeownership deserves more subsidy than renting, whether capitalization into house prices offsets benefits, and whether grandfathering existing mortgages helps reliance interests.
entries.details: Source asks whether homeownership deserves more subsidy than renting, whether capitalization into house prices offsets benefits, and whether grandfathering existing mortgages helps reliance interests.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 12 Chapter 10 pp.540–542

entries.title: Distributional homeownership context
entries.summary: Text reports 2017 racial homeownership gaps and housing cost burdens relevant to policy debate.
entries.laymanExplanation: A deduction mainly used by owners can distribute benefits unevenly where ownership rates differ by group.
entries.legalExplanation: Textbook shows 2017 rates and costs, historical descriptive data only. The figures are not current 2026 demographics and are context rather than a tax-law test.
entries.details: Textbook shows 2017 rates and costs, historical descriptive data only. The figures are not current 2026 demographics and are context rather than a tax-law test.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 12 Chapter 10 pp.542

entries.title: §164 SALT itemized deduction
entries.summary: Qualifying state/local income or sales taxes plus eligible property taxes are itemized, subject to overall cap and MAGI reduction.
entries.laymanExplanation: State income and property taxes may reduce federal taxable income, but not without limits.
entries.legalExplanation: §164 allows certain personal state/local taxes on Schedule A. Individual chooses sales tax OR state/local income tax, not both; business expense tax rules differ. Casebook's $10k cap is outdated for 2026.
entries.details: §164 allows certain personal state/local taxes on Schedule A. Individual chooses sales tax OR state/local income tax, not both; business expense tax rules differ. Casebook's $10k cap is outdated for 2026.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 12 Chapter 10 pp.543–545

legalWarning.label: 2026 SALT CAP $40,400
legalWarning.reason: Book's $10,000 cap and post-2025 sunset forecast are outdated. IRS states 2026 limit $40,400 ($20,200 MFS), subject to MAGI phase-down above $505,000 ($252,500 MFS) but not below $10,000 ($5,000 MFS).

entries.title: §164(b)(5) income-tax vs sales-tax election
entries.summary: Individual cannot claim both state/local general sales tax and state/local income tax for same year.
entries.laymanExplanation: If you live in Florida, choosing sales taxes can be useful because there is no personal state income tax.
entries.legalExplanation: Itemizer elects either state/local income tax or general sales tax under §164(b)(5); qualifying real estate/personal property taxes generally separate and included in aggregate cap.
entries.details: Itemizer elects either state/local income tax or general sales tax under §164(b)(5); qualifying real estate/personal property taxes generally separate and included in aggregate cap.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 12 Chapter 10 pp.544–545

entries.title: Pass-through entity tax (PTET) workaround
entries.summary: State taxes entity-level partnership/S corporation income to permit potential federal business deduction outside individual SALT limits.
entries.laymanExplanation: A law firm partnership may pay state tax at the firm level rather than only its partners' returns.
entries.legalExplanation: Casebook notes some states' elective entity taxes and tax regulation treatment; availability/credits and federal classification depend on state rules and IRS guidance.
entries.details: Casebook notes some states' elective entity taxes and tax regulation treatment; availability/credits and federal classification depend on state rules and IRS guidance.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 12 Chapter 10 pp.543–544

entries.title: SALT ability-to-pay versus subsidy rationales
entries.summary: Deduction may reflect involuntary taxes or subsidize state services; opponents note local benefits and uneven distribution.
entries.laymanExplanation: Should a federal taxpayer get a deduction because their state charges higher taxes? It's a policy question.
entries.legalExplanation: Textbook discusses local public services, intergovernmental fiscal effects and state revenue distribution; not itself a legal eligibility rule.
entries.details: Textbook discusses local public services, intergovernmental fiscal effects and state revenue distribution; not itself a legal eligibility rule.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 12 Chapter 10 pp.544–545

entries.title: §151 personal exemption deduction set to zero in 2026
entries.summary: Pre-2018 personal exemptions allowed per person/dependent; 2026 amount remains zero after permanent 2025 legislation.
entries.laymanExplanation: You cannot currently claim the old separate $4,050-per-person exemption on top of standard deduction.
entries.legalExplanation: Textbook asserts personal exemptions would return after 2025. Current law makes the §151 personal exemption amount zero permanently beginning 2026, though dependent status still matters for other credits/filing status.
entries.details: Textbook asserts personal exemptions would return after 2025. Current law makes the §151 personal exemption amount zero permanently beginning 2026, though dependent status still matters for other credits/filing status.

legalWarning.label: PERSONAL EXEMPTIONS NOT RESTORED
legalWarning.reason: Book anticipates revival of §151 personal exemptions in 2026; 2025 law permanently maintains zero. IRS confirms 2026 and 2027 zero.

entries.title: Dependent — §152 qualifying child/relative rules
entries.summary: Person meeting qualifying-child or qualifying-relative relationship, residency, age, support and other statutory tests.
entries.laymanExplanation: Your dependent isn't simply anyone you're paying money to support.
entries.legalExplanation: Casebook sketches qualifying children under 19 or under 24 if qualifying full-time student, plus qualifying relatives. Actual §152 has multiple requirements; dependent status remains relevant to child-related credits and head of household even with §151 zero amount.
entries.details: Casebook sketches qualifying children under 19 or under 24 if qualifying full-time student, plus qualifying relatives. Actual §152 has multiple requirements; dependent status remains relevant to child-related credits and head of household even with §151 zero amount.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 12 Chapter 10 pp.545–546

entries.title: Standard deduction doesn't directly increase with number of dependents
entries.summary: Replacing personal exemptions with larger standard deduction changed relative treatment of families of different sizes.
entries.laymanExplanation: Two families with same filing status generally get the same basic standard deduction even if one has more kids.
entries.legalExplanation: Textbook argues 2017 substitution of larger standard deduction for personal exemptions can disadvantage larger households absent other credits; this is policy context, not a separate deduction eligibility rule.
entries.details: Textbook argues 2017 substitution of larger standard deduction for personal exemptions can disadvantage larger households absent other credits; this is policy context, not a separate deduction eligibility rule.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 12 Chapter 10 pp.545–546
